sample_q_texts: Modeling the evolution of light and structure in an active aurora explained the development of highly fluctuating auroral magnetic fields that aid convection. Natural noise can propagate to ion compositions and dramatically alter future weather, producing particularly strong auroras and "auroral storms." The accuracy with which earlier models include noise in general plasmas has not been addressed. Here, we use a two-ion species model to demonstrate how other species of ions -- despite producing similarly changing cloud particles -- can break into turbulence and lead to dramatic weather changes in models that would otherwise be chaos. Future studies incorporating real weather data are recommended.

Ever since the discovery of satellite clusters in galaxies the question of natal seeding of the population has been studied in connection with environmental parameters, star formation rate and evolution. Using the central regions of 20 late-type spirals, I measure the angular momentum of stellar components to constrain the initial properties of the stellar population. I find an angular momentum exceeding 1000 for a spiral component with A=20 kpc. This result implies that the number of the component at birth is greater than the constituent star formation rate (SFR) of the entire system. Analysis of the radial velocity (RV) distribution of the component highlights the intrinsic importance of rotational axis orientation for large scale structures. The rotational axis in this component is anti-parallel to the velocity vector of the spiral arm, and I propose that the super-Sun induced acceleration drives star formation.

Robust implementation of analysis pipelines is a key need in Earth science research. Yet, seismic interferometry remains constrained by noisy data and limited bandwidth, making its application to high-resolution local changes difficult. Lidar thermal cross correlation analysis of seismic records leverages thermal energy measured in reanalyzed observations to derive height and velocity estimates at 3-D sites. Here, we compare co-located cross correlation observations, to determine the accuracy of height estimates made with this method. Results from earthquakes demonstrate the ability to trace variations in height estimates from 0.2 mm to over 1.0 m using very low velocity data, and suggest that improved processing of 0.1 mm data and use of raw Lidar data can strengthen this signal.

Singular Gaussian transitions are nonlinear wave phenomena that have a unique behavior in large amplitudes. They create a gradient in the noise density and are found in a wide variety of wave systems that include nonreciprocal nonlinearities and dispersive modes. At high amplitudes they go through a threshold point where nonlinear behavior switches to all-gain dynamics. As a result, we used an ADM-SAO time-scale experiment to build a statistical understanding of such threshold dynamics and generate an analytical response function for Gaussian resonance. By incorporating multiresolution analysis, we are able to assign the threshold to an asymptotic behavior for a large constant N step size. The strength of the resonances is then found as an energy parameter for a limited N range. We propose that for low threshold amplitudes, nonlinear evolution with N can be approximated as Taylor series expansion of a scaling function that depends on the local sound speed and the nonlinear damping coefficient, of the first two Taylor moments. Additionally, we present and study new non-linear wave phenomena in a transonic Mach-number flow. As the Mach number increases, the wave is transformed into lossy behaviors with lower wave vectors and higher amplitude. These transitions are explained as singular Gaussian transition in energy with threshold-like behavior.

As Earths global surface air temperature has risen by a magnitude commensurate with climate models, over 90% of the past 57 decades have been cooler than the 1951-1980 pre-industrial base line. Temperature records at the geographical scale of cities and the regional level of countries continue to reveal a higher-temperature history than in previous decades. Yet, to date, there are insufficient data to fully reconstruct the temperature record for the decade-to-century (or higher) timescale. Here, we produce detailed historical temperature time series at the city and country level to allow for the enhanced clarity of past climate variability. Cities dominate global temperature variations as they store a wide range of regional precipitation and surface flux data; yet, the missing layers of air temperature response control over the scale of resolution remains. To address the climate challenges, a novel ensemble technique with high-temporal (monthly) resolution is developed. The ability to repeat the dataset using this time resolution will enable the assessment of model robustness and validate observed variations. Finally, we developed a framework to enforce persistence conditions of past states to limit the effects of high-frequency signal variation and extend the historical reference period into the future. As a result, the present is treated as the final state in a quasistable regime for over 100 years with coarse temporal resolution that significantly reduces the risk of nonlinear filtering from high-frequency variability. The policy of attempting to diagnose past climate with the present bias therefore needs to be implemented accordingly.

Radiant energy emitted from the sun is one of the most important natural solar factors. Hence, understanding the role of the Sun in the ice ages and its feedback on the climate is of great importance. While helioseismology has proven to be a compelling approach for addressing ice age investigations, the challenges inherent in deriving decadal magnetic field variations in the solar interior remain substantial. An alternate approach, using biostimulation techniques, has emerged as a valuable tool for elucidating electromagnetic interactions within Earths magnetosphere. By manipulating the frequency of background radio signals through synchronized exposure to varying solar stimuli, magnetic field changes can be observed and tracked. Leveraging new information extracted from the decoding algorithms of Kalman filters, this research project introduces two novel features of magnetohydrodynamic simulations: a three-wavelength Kalman filter aimed at frequency modulation and a polyphasic excitation for frequency-varying fields. Employing the new features, 554 magnetometer periods of [DE3371934930] were decontaminated. Coupled with these enhancements, this project provides a valuable ground for experimentation as an alpha-production (alphaP) and the first-of-its-kind experiment designed to enable measurements of second-order fluctuations in various gamma-ray burst explosions (GRBs) in the solar neighborhood.

Nitrous oxide (NO) is a ubiquitous greenhouse gas which produces negligible warming during its short half-life, yet it exerts global climate effects by persistent tropospheric and stratospheric photolysis, which can induce collisions with clouds and may weaken radiation or cause the exhalation of certain volatile organic compounds (VOCs). NO photolysis rates as a function of wavelength have been measured at a number of stations and are in general a log-linear function of emission wavelength, with strong slopes in ambient air for free NO and strongly suppressed or nearly non-existent for heterogeneously formed NO. NO photolysis at 15.4nm can be approximated by an exponentially decreasing function with a slope determined by the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. It has long been hypothesized that photolysis of NO should affect the concentration of absorbing atmospheric aerosols, such as black carbon (BC) and organic carbon (OC), and could lead to a stronger local radiative forcing by these aerosols.

Here, we conduct laboratory measurements of NO photolysis rates and electron affinity, determine the best fit, and calculate the relative intensity ratios of oxidized and elemental atmospheric fluxes of NO. We find that NO photolysis effects these ratios and show that they can alter BC and OC concentrations. We estimate that high NO concentrations would suppress BC formation via multiple routes while slowing down production of tropospheric OC. This would lead to a lower fraction of OC in the troposphere and may offset some of the emission of OC from bare soil and biomass fires.

If atmospheric responses of NO photolysis to increasing NO concentrations turn out to be substantial, this will shift atmospheric composition and climate feedback to rapidly rise in the future. This signal is largely undetected today because of current measurement resolutions, especially at O3-resonant wavelengths. The strong enhancement of NO photolysis with longer wavelengths of NO (at 15.4 nm) makes this measurement essential for addressing the relevance of atmospheric NO photolysis for climate and emerging climate science.

Environmental magnetic fields of terrestrial planets affect their magnetic field in many ways. Since large planets transport their magnetic fields by planet-scale currents, it is interesting to explore the coupling between their planetary magnetic field and the internal currents induced in the planetary core by these magnetospheric currents. In this study, we address the interaction of planetary currents that are generated by atmospheric convection and planetary magnetosphere by a model planet. We find that at latitudes closer than 5 degrees, the chaotic mag- netospheric current has a much stronger influence on planetary convection than a simple molecular convection driven by the radial temperature gradient. The terrestrial core-mantle coupling will thus be deeper and more significant than previously assumed. We find that the planetary magnetic flux produces a magnetic force that stretches the core inner boundary to as much as 1.62 GM; consequently the core-mantle boundary that we derive from this mechanism moves significantly toward the core interior. For a given geodynamo model, our results point to a physical mechanism that manifests in ways that can be difficult to predict based on classical models. These findings are important for constructing climate models, and in situ observations of terrestrial planetary-scale magnetic fields.

The bird communal roosts are mediated by highly-organized social processes, including flight of individual birds across the sound barrier. This acoustic communication is initiated upon contact at the nest platform by the alarm-giver bird, which also decides the alarm bandwidth. Sound propagation in a complex acoustic system is reflected in the local collective behavior of the birds. Here, we manipulate our bird model by experimentally building sound-imitating loudspeakers inside and behind the sound-defying materials (SFM). 1) The acoustic signal's repetition and interference are reduced by sound-defying materials due to the reduced sound loss and scattering. 2) We find the birds alter their acoustic frequency responses according to the local reverberation times. 3) For natural sound-defying materials, we find that the birds alter their behavior to reach a higher frequency range during the maxima phase. We find these results have potential applications for industrial noise mitigation in birds, cities and aerial acoustics and are reproducible results with similar response.

IMPORTANCEThe patterns in the acoustic frequency responses of the birds have been reported under natural sound-defying materials to originate from the collective evolution and interactions among the individuals and their interactions. These have been explored by investigating the birds in the social roosts at a cluster level, revealing novel architecture with the bird-bird interaction. However, this has yet to be investigated in small populations, i.e. single birds. Here, we applied the methodology of the sound-defying materials to a simple avian community in order to experimentally reveal what patterns this can support. Our finding suggests a fundamental architectural feature to the social roosts, which depends on the sound-defying materials in nature, for providing collective roosting in a narrow frequency band.

Statistical density estimators, which estimate quantities of interest at points in the high dimensional space, such as the spectral density in high dimensional measurements. Classical modes such as Spectral Quadrupole and Spectral Principal Components method (SPCM) are commonly applied. However, these arise from the linear correlation of the histogram distribution. Due to high dimensionality, and the correlations between points, the distribution to be estimated may be highly non-Gaussian. In this work, we developed a two-dimensional density estimator, which respects the whole histogram distribution and is clearly non-Gaussian. We also apply the estimator to wave excitation and spectral inversion problems. Our approach is used to study and predict the energy dependent effect of subwavelength metal lines. We also apply it to the spectral reconstruction of minerals and thus to "calibrate" the known mineral spectral densities. The empirical approach allows for rapid calculation of density estimates of spectral line and expected spectral signals, and is thus attractive in the spectral domain.

A gut microbiome in the human fetus is shaped by maternal immune responses that are shaped by maternal nutrition and lifestyle. The influence of the microbiome on the development of the fetus is of growing importance for understanding the development of later life metabolic disorders and inflammatory diseases such as obesity, diabetes, and atherosclerosis. The human microbiome is a continuously developing ecosystem of bacteria, viruses, and fungi that lives on all organs. In addition, it can inhabit the gut microbiome of other animals. Due to its organ specificity, it is difficult to study microbiome-gut microbiota interactions using basic human cell lines. To model the human gut microbiome, we developed artificial gut microbes as a non-human, pathogen-free host. We developed the smallest functional read mix from the human microbiome, comprising the largest strains we have cultured and characterized. With the help of different modeling techniques we gained insight into the relationship between bacteria in the gut microbiome and the development of offspring. The combination of classical and novel methods helps to understand the role of the bacterial microbiome on the development of offspring and sheds light on the interrelationships of the gut microbiome with obesity, diabetes, and atherosclerosis and their impact on human health.

The evolution of microbial life has been shaped by environmental stresses, especially the avoidance of deleterious mutations. This phenomenon has been observed across organisms, including humans. Here, we provide evidence that perceptual experiences during pre-implantation development, including the recognition of well-protected and ill-protected organs, are critical for adaptive immune development and evasion of exogenous pathogens. In mice, mice that lacked the pawepril gene were prone to infectious protozoa-induced pneumonia, even if they escaped mucosal disease in their primary environment. Premices were similarly deficient in invasive infections when they developed a specific littermate and in germ-free mice exposed to pathogens. Premices showed increased escape tolerance toward pathogens but were less able to resist pneumonia. Crucially, this enhanced tolerance was also present in premesial mice at high pathogen density. Additionally, in contrast to their response to respiratory infections, mice lacking the pawepril gene tended to show decreased impairment of predatory behaviour, highlighting the importance of defenses against pathogens as well as against predation. These results point to potential future pathogen-specific therapies for a range of infectious diseases.

SignificanceStatement
Immune evasion requires certain behaviors, e.g. inactivity during infection, in order to dampen disease progression. Yet individual tolerance to pathogens results in enhanced immune activity during pathogen exposure. Here, we show the evolution of perceptual immune mechanisms during development, when organisms are less protected against pathogens in their environment. We show that this tolerance has specific benefits but does not always allow survival in stressed conditions, particularly pathogens that evade the development defenses in development. Notably, this might be essential for survival in germ-free mice and for humans exposed to polluted environments.

Lower gut microbiota has been implicated in obesity, particularly in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM), but the exact mechanisms remain unclear. Gut microbiota can enter the circulatory system through the blood-gut barrier and enter the brain via the Enteric Nervous System (ENS). We explored how the microbiota in the upper digestive tract (UDT) influences food-driven changes in the microbiota in the lower intestine (GIL). Healthy mice were fed a chow diet (DDD) for 4 weeks. We assessed changes in microbiota in the GIT, blood, and brain following changes in the intestinal microbial phenotype over 12 weeks. Our study found that an excessive diet increased microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in the GIT, which increased salivary [L-carnitine methyltransferase (LCMT; human), 5-methyltetrahydrofolate methyltransferase (5MTHFD; human), pancreatic lipase (PL) in the upper digestive tract (UDT) but not in the lower digestive tract (LDT). In contrast, we found that the diet reduced microbiota in the UDT compared to that in the LDT. Further, the diet enhanced the expression of PL and LCFT in the LDT compared to the UDT, highlighting distinct influences in the UDT and LDT. Moreover, we found an increase in glycolysis-induced SCFA synthesis in the lower intestine (GIL) after the diet, as well as an increase in a mixed fermentation, where fermenters included bacteria (Actinobacterium opariforme, Lalogenitoloxydodecanoat, Pediococcus pentosaceus, Bacillus infantis, Alcaligenes), fungi (Ashospirillum kumirai, Botrytis sinopleuceti, Candida lipolytica, Mortierella alpina), and yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). In short, our results imply that exposure to a high-fat diet induces fecal SCFA production in the lower GI tract, followed by associated metabolic and nutrient changes. However, these effects are transient and can be eliminated when the gut microbiota and SCFA (short-chain fatty acids) are re-established.

Breastfeeding can be an important factor in child survival for mother and child. Obesity is a serious risk factor for diabetes and impaired infant health. Diabetes, especially, is associated with a range of adverse infant outcomes. One of the main concern is the abnormal development of the glycocaline and delta-aminobutyric acid (GABA) systems in infants of diabetic mothers. Alpha-lactalbumin is an important glycoprotein in breastmilk that may contribute to this environment. Building on this, here, we investigated the effects of antibody isolated from a breastfed rat or mouse in a rat pre-adipocyte co-culture system. The groups contained maternal milk or rat or mouse sera, respectively. The animals that consumed the rat sera had a significantly higher level of interleukin (IL)-10 and interferon (IFN) gamma. Additionally, IL-10 and IL-12 mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in the G19 group of the infant mouse liver. Interestingly, levels of lactalbumin and the fatty acid delta-12-lipoic acid were much higher in the G19 group. Also, lactation milk exposure at the P361pstPAh score (i.e., the 14th or 15th or 16th day after birth) inhibited breast growth and prevented the birthweight gain of the newborn rats and mouse offspring. However, the same exposure led to significantly higher glucocorticoid levels at the P361pstPAh score and higher levels of expression of the SREBP-1-BP1 signaling pathway in the mouse neonate. Increased beta-adrenergic sensitivity (measured by circulating concentrations of catecholamines) and reduced cortisol release as well as neuropeptide Y expression were reported. Breastfeeding from an adult mouse, with a bacterial colony, and then fed, had an immediate short-term increase in the expression of the IL-10 cytokine, interleukin-21, interferon-gamma, as well as alpha-lactalbumin levels. Long-term breastfed newborn rats demonstrated increased abundance of G19 and reduced beta-adrenergic receptor (band 3) and decreased somatostatin expression in the liver. These findings show that for acute animal skin and liver exposures, postnatal growth may be enhanced through the proinflammatory system in breastfed rats. The study also showed that breastfed neonatal mouse livers have an enhanced influx of serotonin and a significant change in GABA signaling, not associated with weight gain or lactation.

We show that the microbiome is crucial for maintaining a healthy state of the intestine and gut functioning, and is crucial for maintaining robust mucosal immune function in the gut. Microbiome disruption alters immunogenicity of foreign antigens in the GI tract, with implications for susceptibility to autoimmune diseases like inflammatory bowel disease. The same disruption also alters normal inflammatory responses and pro-inflammatory cytokines in the presence of normal commensal microbiota. These changes in both the immunity at mucosal sites and systemic immunity create opportunities for emerging infections. Understanding the impact of the microbiome on a variety of hosts such as healthy individuals and those undergoing other therapies (e.g., transplant recipients) will greatly expand the opportunities for GI treatment, transplantation, or vaccine development.

Evidence shows that human-gut microbiota contribute to the successful colonization and establishment of a diverse human microbiota in humans. Studies exploring interactions between germline microbial influences and host immunological responses are insufficient; however, many phenotypes associated with susceptibility to bacterial infection such as skin infections and asthma are diseases dominated by viral and bacterial diseases, and exposure to viruses during viral infections, such as early infants, can have various health consequences. Therefore, studying interactions between the innate immune system and the gut microbiota may help to elucidate possible mechanisms underlying these health outcomes. Identifying the association between the immature immune system and the gut microbiota is crucial for our understanding of the roles of gut microbes in the protection of infants from severe respiratory diseases. In this study, the composition of the gut microbiome was investigated in preterm infant feces and maternal feces, to explore whether maternal microbial immunity effects offspring preterm infant microbiota in the intestinal mucosa (through the microbiota-immune system link). The results showed that early preterm infants had higher abundance of Prevotellacausalvelly enriched in the mucosa of the small intestine and mucosal-associated (M1) and tissue-associated (M2) intestinal bacterial composition. Genotyping of P. bactericus strains revealed that the infants had enriched Staphyloccoccosisinfusiseslis-related (MiRL) and Acinetobacterfiumaccescence (MicrR-step). We also found that P. bactericus strains may be associated with respiratory diseases such as asthma in early preterm infants.

Recent evidence suggests that sleep plays a critical role in gut microbiota composition. However, understanding the molecular mechanisms that underpin this relationship remains incomplete. This study systematically examined changes in gut microbiota and mucosal bacterial proteins during sleep in mice fed a high-fat/high-sucrose diet (HFHS). One sleep stage was used as the baseline for each subject for comparison. Monitoring bacterial mRNA expression by RNA sequencing across all mice allowed us to identify gene changes in neutrophils, Kupffer cells, and intestinal epithelium as well as eosinophils. Tissue RNase protection assays showed that mucosal cytokines, such as IL-17, IFN-gamma, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and transforming growth factor-beta were all detectable at detectable levels in the infiltrating cells. In contrast, only a few gene changes were identified in the intestinal epithelium and macrophages, including KLK5, IL-23, IL-22, and IL-23R. Our results suggest that both the environmental factors present during sleep - circadian pattern, sleep phase, time of day - and the physiological components such as NF-кB, IL-17, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and transforming growth factor-beta are critical for sleep-associated bacterial regulation. A similar effect was demonstrated in hamsters, but it was not observed in adult mice.

Newborn infants rely on mother-specific bacteria, given birth to in the mother's uterus, for nourishment, protection, and microbiota. Breast milk transports these bacteria for the infant's microbiota, but does it also contain the protective elements of microbiota by providing for mammary stem cells? We are interested in how maternal bacteria and microbiota influence breast milk and newborns to assure they are optimal microbiome-immune profiles as well as optimal health outcomes. To answer this, our work is comparing uterine and postnatal microbiota from different maternal bacterial strains (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Bacteroides, and Fusobacterium). Analysis of bacterial genetics, gene expression, and metabolomics in uterine and postnatal samples will provide evidence that bacteria and microbiota influence breast milk and newborns to serve as optimal microbiome-immune profiles as well as optimal health outcomes. This will identify optimal bacteria and/or microbiota for early immune priming (e.g. faster virus clearance) and for developing immune systems (e.g. longer and healthier life expectancy).

In response to shocks from microbiota-derived nutrients, gut homeostasis is affected by a shift from intestinal homeostatic regulation to increased growth of harmful bacteria. Gut bacterial composition in turn impacts the human microbiome and alters host metabolism by regulating intestinal motility. We sought to understand the effects of differential bacterial profiles in mouse gut microbiota on local pH, luminal microenvironment, and systemic gut homeostasis. We found that a significant bacterial composition shift in mouse adult feeding is sufficient to initiate self-perpetuating metabolic dysregulation by altering intestinal microbial metabolic capacity to metabolize fibers. Specifically, a probiotic model diet with 90% by weight dietary fiber decreased the fecal microbial diversity of the experimental mice by deleting bacterial metabolic capabilities for detaching and cell-surface-present fibers. By reducing soluble pectin and fiber-neutralizing bacteria in the distal gut mucosa and altering pro-tumoral shifts in the gut microbiome, the mice infected with Lactobacillus acidophilus re-established gut homeostasis by depleting the microbiota shift during weaned weaning and subsequent bacterial re-establishment. These results uncover a mechanism by which prebiotic fiber detaches fiber from the host and stores it in the gut lumen where it contributes to metabolic dysregulation. Our studies thus show that gut bacteria responsible for fiber digestion are involved in shaping the post-weaning microbiome and its ability to maintain gut homeostasis.

The microbiome plays a key role in shaping gut health and obesity, but little is known about whether changes in the microbial composition of the gut and on the skin are important in these connections. We assessed the associations between skin bacteria, through the trans-epithelial adherence index, and gut bacteria, via the host microbiota overlap between the microbiota of the skin and gut. Skin bacteria were associated with the microbiota of the skin via host diet. However, in individuals with both atopic dermatitis (AD) and obesity, the only significant associations we found were between AD and total volatiles from the skin and the gut. These associations were accompanied by crosstalk between the skin and gut microbiota. We further show that overgrowth of bacteria from the skin microbiome exacerbates atopic symptoms in high-fat-high-calorie (HFC) diet-induced mice. These findings suggest that the mutual connections of microbiota represent key mechanisms linking the skin and gut microbiomes and contribute to its dysfunction in AD and obesity.

BackgroundThe microorganisms colonizing the gastrointestinal tract of animals, collectively referred to as the gut microbiome, affect numerous host behaviors dependent on the central nervous system (CNS). Studies comparing germ-free mice to normally colonized mice have demonstrated influences of the microbiome on anxiety-related behaviors, voluntary activity, and gene expression in the CNS. Additionally, there is epidemiologic evidence supporting an intergenerational influence of the maternal microbiome on neurodevelopment of offspring and behavior later in life. There is limited experimental evidence however directly linking the maternal microbiome to long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, or knowledge regarding mechanisms responsible for such effects.

ResultsHere we show that that the maternal microbiome has a dominant influence on several offspring phenotypes including anxiety-related behavior, voluntary activity, and body weight. Adverse outcomes in offspring were associated with features of the maternal microbiome including bile salt hydrolase activity gene expression (bsh), abundance of certain bile acids, and hepatic expression of Slc10a1. In cross-foster experiments, offspring resembled their birth dam phenotypically, despite faithful colonization in the postnatal period with the surrogate dam microbiome. Genome-wide methylation analysis of hippocampal DNA identified microbiome- associated differences in methylation of 196 loci in total, 176 of which show conserved profiles between mother and offspring. Further, single-cell transcriptional analysis revealed accompanying differences in expression of several differentially methylated genes within certain hippocampal cell clusters, and vascular expression of genes associated with bile acid transport.

Inferred cell-to-cell communication in the hippocampus based on coordinated ligand-receptor expression revealed differences in expression of neuropeptides associated with satiety.

ConclusionsCollectively, these data provide proof-of-principle that the maternal gut microbiome has a dominant influence on the neurodevelopment underlying certain offspring behaviors and activities, and selectively affects genome methylation and gene expression in the offspring CNS in conjunction with that neurodevelopment.

AbstractTo achieve immune and microbial homeostasis during adulthood, the developing immune system must learn to identify which microbes to tolerate and which to defend against. How such  immune education unfolds remains a major knowledge gap. We address this gap by synthesizing existing literature to develop a mechanistic mathematical model representing the interplay between gut ecology and adaptive immunity in early life. Our results indicate that the inflammatory tone of the microenvironment is the mediator of information flow from pre- to post- weaning periods. We evaluate the power of postnatal fecal samples for predicting immunological trajectories, and explore breastfeeding scenarios when maternal immunological conditions affect breastmilk composition. Our work establishes a quantitative basis for immune education, yielding insights into questions of applied relevance.

sample_q_texts: Parapsychological phenomena refer to observations about mind-world relations, mind-mind relations, and mind-body relations, notably ascribing paranormal skills, abilities, talents, phenomena, personal transformations, and so forth to paranormal entities. Popular beliefs have long pointed towards parapsychological phenomena of possession and telekinesis (i.e. the mind-body distinction), yet the full set of claims, parapsychological entities, and phenomena, remain a highly contested area of psychological and social debate. Current research shows that a wide range of parapsychological phenomena, including spirits and ghosts, mediumship and psychokinesis, clairvoyance, mediums, demon possession, artificial field phenomena, and artificial intelligence, are not described by the dispositional (i.e. general) parapsychological model, but rather by the particular person perception (PP) model. A PP model is thus developed which explicates such phenomena from a parapsychological perspective and demonstrates how a "recognizer" can acquire different abilities to recognize person perceptions as both identical and different from internal personal states. The present study utilized the PSPP model to analyze the phenomena of clairvoyance, mediumship, telepathy, and psychokinesis (e.g. mind-body relations) from a parapsychological perspective. The data consisted of two audiovisual transcripts of clairvoyance phenomena reported by a German medium, and five utterances by a German medium who claimed being haunted by a demon. The findings show that the findings agree with the PSPP model in a probabilistic way: Supernatural entities have different types of transformations according to two class-type criteria.

More people than ever are seeking to establish strong connections to nature for their own mental health benefits. Virtual nature experiences can promote connection but have not been studied for their impacts on attention. We explored the effects of a virtual outdoor urban view (XOUV) experience, previously shown to encourage nature-based stress reduction, on feature detection, which can influence attention control. Participants (n = 21, 2.81 = 0.95) engaged in 6 XOUVs using a longitudinal mixed method design, with imaging technology following remote point cloud data, measuring eye position, fixation rate and display annoyance and mental awareness using in vivo behavioral, physiological and mind-wandering measures. Feature detection time was significantly lower on XOUVs than on simulacra (---34.19, ----28.14). Fine-scale scene detail such as bricks, walls and protruding windows significantly enhanced error detection, while an accumulation of natural scenes showed little to no effect. However, fine-scale non-visuality (such as a lack of noise in the forest or distant rooftops) increased when visual clarity was maintained in the backdrop. Differences in feature detection times were better predicted by feature quality: natural and urban scenes were more error-prone than near or far scenes or rural and urban (xia)-naturals, and, surprisingly, granular microenvironment details were more error-prone than macro-environment details. A greater degree of feature complexity generally promotes error, particularly at finer spatial scales. These results suggest that different levels of visual clarity of a real-world natural or urban environment can cause greater attentional demand during feature detection than greater visual complexity. Feature complexity also promoted error in fine-scale scene detail, likely due to distraction or the use of more central visual regions. However, detailed landscapes promoted less error in fine-scale spatial detail, likely due to increased self-focused awareness and decreased dominance of attention recovery. These results expand the role of feature complexity and detail variation in web-based immersive and augmented environment experiences to direct further research.

Orthodox beliefs about environmental challenges, particularly the potential of beliefs and media misinformation as drivers of social networks, shape well-being. However, much about how beliefs can lead to misinformation remain opaque. This study presents a comprehensive examination of assumptions made by lay respondents from 14 countries involved in a real-world public narrative experiment. Data analysis revealed that individuals displaying less evidence-based beliefs (expressing more confidence in traditional vs. expert knowledge) were significantly more likely to share misleading media content, regardless of whether they felt more strongly about a particular challenge (e.g., harm vs. beneficial management). Conversely, individuals with more evidence-based beliefs displayed less likelihood to share misinformation when compared with those with more limited evidence-based beliefs. Our findings challenge the conventional wisdom that evidence-based beliefs are beneficial for health and well-being, suggesting that research priorities may need to shift in line with more complex societal realities.

The absence of a vital text icon in the cell message panel frustrates users in many current cell biology applications. Conventional solutions include overlaying an intentional invisible text icon below or above the cellular text, but this compromise results in unnecessary confusion. Here, we present a user study showing that fixing the visual appearance of the cell message panel is a viable solution to promoting intuitive content analysis through a new cell path diagram application. Guided by our findings, we designed an applet to implement a visual contrast between the tabular data and the box of the cellular message panel. Performance metrics for initial ratings of the applet, as compared to a button-based option, indicate that the applet performs equally well as the button, while contributing to improved aesthetics by positioning the text and custom icons within the visual design of the cell message panel. A large acceptance ratio showed that the visual redesign enabled users to recognize and reach important information in the cell message panel by focusing on the bottom-right position of the box and the tiny cell message panel on the right-hand side. In contrast, unoptimized existing options do not inform users about the important information in the text menu and are difficult to locate visually on the right-hand side in a scrolling block. Ultimately, we established a new design approach in cellular communications to inform the appearance and positioning of complex information in medical information panel applications.

Identifying factors influencing how individuals respond to medical interventions or exposures to hazards is essential to improving risk communication and situational awareness. Self-governance is increasingly relied upon in this context, with individualized insights into a person's personal and social characteristics. The application of such self-governance-based interventions is growing in importance in both real-world scenarios and virtual environments. A single repository for all contextual health risk profiles used across these different applications is thus desired. To date, however, no dedicated repository has been developed. This study applies two specific strategies: (1) multi-disciplinary collaboration to integrate risk intelligence input from various domains, including health, social sciences, natural sciences, and humanities, and (2) theory-driven design to harness the strengths of different contextual health risk profiles into a single, comprehensive database. Using three action films spanning action thriller, war drama, and family drama genres, we leveraged an interdisciplinary editorial team composed of composers, screenwriters, artists, and actors to produce a checklist of risk cues across all four contexts. These checklists were iteratively composed by a virtual editorial team and refined to address contextual, sociodemographic, and visual-kinetic risks in a series of three-step open calls. Each call featured a set of conceptual drafts for actors and collaborators to refine prior to a final round of design, resulting in multiple different sets of draft checklists that were ranked and ranked-up. The resulting checklist represented a novel approach to contextual health risk profile databases and their related content, validating the framework as a robust design tool in virtual environments.

Human-centricity refers to a childs(cid:468;s) perceptual experience that is focused on the childs(cid:468;s) own interests. For example, an app for toddlers could offer sensory motor stimulation with lights and sounds. Metaphorically, the childs[cid:468;s] perspective on the parent or caregiver could be made clear by a touch screen. Human-centeredity is human-centeredness when the way a product is designed, manufactured, distributed and deployed is considered from the perspective of the people whom it is intended to serve and the people whose behaviors influence the product in various ways. Human-centered technology is referred to as the most important tool to enhance human health. In this paper, we introduce the general framework for the human-centered design of health and medicine through an ethical approach to empower the designer and to establish a human-centered design of medicine framework.

Whereas human-centered design is crucial to designing products that improve peoples[cid:468;s] health and wellbeing, the design of human-centric medical technology requires a new model and a new methodology to achieve this goal. Health must be contextualized and designed at the intersection of user- and device-centeredness, in order to design technology for users that have positive effects on the user and for users who can design the technology that is contextualized for the user. This enables design to be translated from its current state, where user-centeredness is focused solely on user health, to focus on user-centeredness for the sake of their health. This paradigm shift facilitates a hybrid design approach that blends user-centeredness and device-centeredness and transforms the concept of human-centered design for the sake of health into a design framework that considers user and device-centeredness, and human-centeredness, as well as the ethical, moral, and legal consequences of such hybrid design.

Changes in how we consume, process, and analyze data can lead to shifts in the patterns of information-sharing networks that characterize today's Social Media technologies. In this paper we use the term algorithmic trading system to describe a shared understanding of "a system of computation and data used to make decisions about economic transactions by stock exchange traders." We identify a growing number of trading-systems-including algorithmic trading platforms and AI algorithms for stock market analysis-used by market makers as well as algorithmic strategies that are deployed by non-market-makers within and between their social networks. As a result, trade execution is moving to more places and at faster speeds than trading volumes and user use-patterns have already driven. AI and the proliferation of algorithmic systems have democratized resource utilization across the spectrum of algorithmic trading systems--including the number of users using those systems. This continues to produce new kinds of problem behavior that threaten profit maximization, and new exploitative profit-extraction models that incorporate those problem behaviors, even though they challenge fundamental algorithmic trading principles.

Traditionally, algorithmic trading-systems have been justified by trade execution-not trade volume, which has been associated with the most profit-maximizing system behavior. We argue, however, that changes in the ways financial markets process and compute trade execution data point to a new kind of profit maximization that privileges liquidity and efficiency at the cost of market equilibrium. This study contributes to a broader literature assessing the limits of algorithmic trading. It also provides a new perspective on how algorithmic trading systems must evolve to overcome the "trading revolution" of capital-market interconnectedness-and the corporate power they represent. It provides an opportunity to examine the roles of algorithmic trading systems within social networks, and provides insights on the extent to which algorithms are accountable for their built-in market power. It also argues for systemic attention to algorithmic trading in financial markets, and cautions against the emergence of a new economy of manipulative brokerage firms that blend algorithmic systems with traditional trading practices and false rationalities.

Roslin Hall aims to develop smart, digital technology to support dementia care in a 21st century context. We create, deliver and evaluate two applications: a voice-based alarm monitor for people who are unable to speak when they leave their bed (Deceptive Alarm Display; DAD), and a narrative based care map application (The CMIMap by Deeplume) for family caregivers (CCMAP). Both were tested on people with dementia and caregivers.

In DAD the mouth open detector uses audio and four on-screen images to detect if the person is talking or crying and to let the user know. If they don't talk for 15 seconds, a series of vibrations, a 'tickle', can be received over two directional speakers, alerting them to come back to the bed. If they still don't respond, a warning beep and vibrating relief pad can be received after 2 minutes.

In CCMap, family caregivers are asked to write a short narrative about how their loved one is doing, describing how activities are going, what their quality of life is. An audio recording is made of a 10-minute conversation of the users narrative, and the two map their image of the user in the CCMap, finding the areas of the house that they frequent. In this way people who use apps or fall out of contact are still supported by ongoing caregivers using an effective way of communicating.

Our app-based intelligent care environments are helping to maintain people with dementia in their homes and making everyday interactions better for everyone.

Significance StatementThe aim of Roslin Hall is to continue developing digital care systems that support the lives of people with dementia, their families and carers through promoting better digital communication. The systems we have prototyped and developed can be used as supporting tools for those with dementia to improve care and quality of life. It is important to note that these systems are not replacements for good communication, but are supportive. However, the research we have undertaken has shown that using the systems described in this paper has increased the lives of both people with dementia and their families, helping them to feel more confident about their family members.

Parents guidance can enhance young childrens confidence and success in reading. However, few studies have explored parents guidance in preschool language settings. In this study, 50 parents, 30 with children in an urban kindergarten that offers lessons in story-based, creative language instruction, and 20 with children that attend a preschool specializing in academic language-based language instruction, completed questionnaires. Group differences were examined using an attention network task, a reading task, and a picture completion task. Parents guidance occurred twice a week through experiences such as reading stories together, discussing pictures in a book, and completing story-based tasks. Using in-depth interview data, parents responses were investigated to better understand parents perspective about reading-based language instruction. Analyses revealed that while parents were aware of the influence of their role on children language growth, some of the small differences between parents and teachers were unexpected. Parents in the urban kindergarten attributed family influences to the small differences in reading. Parents in the preschool shared similar explanations for small differences in language between parents and teachers, but did not argue for or against specific roles for these influences in language learning. Parents in both settings reported that parents guidance had little impact on their childrens reading development. These results underscore the importance of exploring non-parental factors and themes associated with academic language and early reading instruction.

Creativity has been defined as the product of a single creative mind, a necessary but not sufficient condition for creativity. An important part of a persons creativity profile is the social aspect of collaboration. Here, we explore this in the development of Western literature with a long tradition of a deconstructivist view on scientific creativity. We will show that collaborative creativity is not necessarily a bad thing, yet it has, and still has, its advantages. These will be discussed in the context of the creativity development theory (Kestler and Holland 2012) and its focus on socio-cultural and social aspects of creativity.
sample_p_texts: Previous research on synchronous movement rituals have found that it increased prosocial propensity toward the synchronised group and reliance on the group opinions. However, whether basic cognitive processes such as perceptual decision-making are affected by synchronous movement remains unexplored. In this novel virtual reality experiment, we examined whether marching synchronously with a group can induce greater informational conformity on an unrelated perceptual task (forced choice random dot motion). We found higher degree of conformity following synchronised marching during low stimulus information. This finding indicates that synchronised movement induces minimal group membership expressed via increased self-other blurring and conformity. Thus, participation in movement-based rituals has the capacity to change our perception of the world to align more closely with the synchronised group.

The personal space in dense crowd situations is commonly underestimated. However, the self-awareness of it can prevent and handle risk situations. The aim of this study was to explore theoretically the use of the personal space as a key concept for designing simple computational models related to collective behaviors and crushing events. We used an agent-based model related to transitional rules associated with the Shellings spatial proximity model of segregation. Based on an explorative data analysis and model validation, we found that the dynamics of crowd events showed significant statistical regularities between dense situations and the individual perception of the personal space. These results suggests that crushing events in dense crowd situations are highly probable and that the density levels are the key for delaying the presence of such disasters.

Many prize synchrony as the ingredient that turns a conversation from a debate into a delightful duet. Yet, learning from other peoples diverging opinions can also foster understanding and agreement, satisfy curiosity, and spur imagination. Using fMRI hyperscanning and natural language processing we tested how two debaters navigate conflictual conversations to find agreement. Dyads (N=60) discussed pressing societal problems while being instructed to either persuade their partner or compromise with each other. Our analysis uncovered three key insights: First, individuals instructed to compromise rather than persuade tended to agree more at the end of the session. Second, hyperscanning and linguistic analyses revealed that encouraging compromise resulted in increased exploration during conversations; dyads given compromise instructions traversed more diverse mental states and topics. Third, heightened exploration was linked to greater eventual agreement. Notably, the effect of the compromise instruction on agreement was entirely mediated by the degree of exploration. Together, these results suggest that trying to find agreement may be spurred by exploration, something that happens when people are motivated to compromise but not persuade.

The ReAct (Recovery, Activity) project is an ENFSI (European Network of Forensic Science Institutes) supported initiative comprising a large consortium of laboratories. Here, the results from more than 23 laboratories are presented. The primary purpose was to design experiments simulating typical casework circumstances; collect data and to implement Bayesian networks to assess the value (i.e., likelihood ratio) of DNA results given activity level propositions. Two different experimental designs were used to simulate a robbery, where a screwdriver was used to force a door or window. Propositions and case information were chosen following laboratory feedback listing typical casework circumstances (included in the paper). Whereas the proposition representing prosecutions view is applicable to many cases: the defendant forced the door/window with his screwdriver; the proposition representing defences view are more variable depending on what is alleged to have happened. In a direct transfer experiment, the defendant owned and used the screwdriver, but he did not force the door/window in question. An unknown person used the defendants stolen screwdriver. In an indirect transfer experiment, the defendant neither owned, saw, nor used the screwdriver, nor did they force the door or window. Instead, an unknown individual--someone with whom the defendant had interacted (e.g., by shaking hands or touching the same objects)--used the recovered tool to force entry. In the first experiment, if the defendant forced the door/window, then s/he is the last handler of the screw driver, whereas if the tool was stolen and used by an unknown person, the defendant is the first handler. For the second experiment, given the defence view, the defendant never held the screwdriver. We envisaged the situation where an object manipulated by the defendant (or the defendant himself/herself) would be touched by the unknown offender who would then force the window. The time delay between the touching of the object and the forcing of the window was 0, 1h, and 2h. This was accomplished by handshaking experiments, where the person forcing the door would shake a persons hand, and then use the screwdriver either immediately after hand-shake or after 1, 2 hours. It was found for the direct transfer experiment that unless a single contributor profile aligning with the known persons of interest profile was retrieved, the results did not allow to discriminate propositions. On the other hand, for the indirect transfer experiment, both single and major contributor profiles that aligned with the person of interest (POI) supported the proposition that the person used the tool rather than an unknown person who had touched an object, when indeed the former was true. There was considerable variation in median recoveries of DNA between laboratories (between 200pg - 5ng) for a given experiment if quantities are taken into account. These differences affect the likelihood ratios given activity level propositions. More than 2,700 samples were analysed in the course of this study. Two different Bayesian Networks are made available via an open source application written in Shiny R: Shiny_React(). For comparison, all datasets were analysed using a qualitative method categorised into absent, single, balanced or major given contributors.

The need for standardisation of methods is highlighted, along with the need for new methods to assess probability of laboratory dependent DNA recovery. Open access databases that are made freely available are important adjuncts

sample_q_texts: Lutetium (Lu) is a rare terrestrial gadolinium analogue with high luminescence, but which requires complex chemical synthesis to obtain high luminescence in luminescent nanorods (LRNs). Hence, these nanomaterials lack a functional substrate to promote photon capture and a necessary level of fundamental understanding of how their luminescent properties are dependent on their chemical composition, thus hindering the transition of the nanoscale luminescent state of the Lu to the clinically appropriate medical regime. Here we designed and synthesized a series of six Y-modified (Y) non-ferrous 1D nano-junctions (Y1DJs) (also known as "Y-junctions" in the literature), corresponding to a plasmonic exchange of the anionic Y-cation, gallium (Ga), in Lu-LRNs, as well as Y2DJs (Y2DJs), based on chemically modified Y. As a model nanomaterial, we explored the spectroscopic properties of Y1DJs and Y2DJs, which were obtained using ultra-broad band X-ray absorption fine-structure (XAFS) spectroscopy. These studies enabled the characterization of quantum dots (QDs), which are not present in the chemical structure of the Y-junction materials, as well as the influence of single-molecule scattering from the Y1DJs (QDs). While the Y2DJs lacked the fluorescent nanoparticles found in the Y1DJs, the Y1DJs did not exhibit any significant impact on the spectrum of the N = 17 resonance line of the fluorophore. Our results highlight the potential of Y-junctions as a new class of ultrasensitive ultrasmall nanoparticles in the field of molecular and functional nanoparticles, a response at the turn of the 20th and 21st centuries.

Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) involves the non-thermal application of a photosensitizing agent for the targeting of diseased tissues. Here, we employ a novel fluorescent nanocomposite of an iridium-based oxygen-emitting quantum dot (O-QD) and a lipid bilayer that is self-assembling. This lipid allows for substrate-specific uptake and stabilization of the O-QD, resulting in rapid and effective differentiation of fluorescent nano-tubes and single-layer cells within tumorous tissue. This new QD-lipid system is able to more effectively distinguish tumor types and highlight the microtubule system, which is involved in axonal transport, thereby influencing the growth of the tumor. This photothermal effect makes this approach a unique tool for PDT applications, namely, developing a photo-responsive functionalized membrane that facilitates enhanced tumor targeting.

Ribosome-driven ExoDYNE assembly appears to be a ubiquitous route to physical-chemical regulation of protein synthesis, forming ribozyme-like domains during ribosomal RNA transcription, translaton, and post-translational modification. How the morphology-and-function interplay of ribosome-driven ExoDYNE can yield complex and various functional outputs has been unclear. Here, we present ultrafast trap-based xylose-acetaldehyde (X+H) physisorbed biosensor employing a carbon-bonded riboswitch-based molecular excitable network (mEZN) as a novel protein:RNA interaction biosensor, which is capable of dynamically changing RNA orientation for synthesizing a zwitterionic ribosomal frameshift framer and regulated ribozyme domains through X+H aggregation. Dynamic assemblies were realized on an ultrasensitive exoDYNE-based ubiquitin E2 Mimic peptide sensor as a device that functioned as a chemo-biological biosensor. X+H interactions based upon edge-to-edge interactions of DNA-protein prodrug trimers stabilized by nucleophiles catalyzed by nucleophilic adenine, phosphodiesterases, and ribozymes. The device can be utilized to make specific RNA conformations at the first ribosome-encoded pro-terminator in mRNA production.

Design logic molecules (DLMs) combine nonlinear materials chemistry, optics, and physics to generate engineered supramolecular materials. Given the increasing importance of detecting disease biomarkers and the need for practical, high-throughput methods, we developed and integrated a LDM-based strategy to generate biosensor devices with potential to overcome speed limitations. These devices function as protein-to-sensor devices, where a protein-sensor "pushes" the LDM into a desired state.
Within the device, a nonvolatile phosphoryl molecule binds to a cysteine residue on a single sensor. Each sensor-side of the device connects to a fluorophore through a linker that enables both, detector and sensor-side, to be accessed. The device response to light serves as the basis of a fluorescent colorimetric sensor readout.
Compared to other known materials-based approaches, the enzymatic activity of the sensor-side is strongly influenced by the ligands on the sensor-side. This property results in sensitive, reversible, and uniform protein-to-sensor devices that are highly stable against enzymatic degradation. Moreover, the strength of the redox-state-driven interferance is tuned by modulating the strength and length of the linker between the sensor-side and the phosphoryl acceptor, allowing simultaneous detection of different proteins of interest in parallel assays.
This prototype device provides an integrated pathway for performing simultaneous differential and sequential protein-to-sensor assays while simultaneously measuring the specific activity of the protein in each case. While this approach enables the detection of very small (Nano-potent) variants of therapeutic proteins, it can be further extended to include the targeting of bulk disordered targets that are protein misfolding diseases.

The Molecular Porphyrin Library (MPL)<sup>1</sup> generates synthetic Porphyrin Chemotypes (PCs) from hundreds of chemical libraries. The results can be assessed to test the PLDS20 algorithm for heterogeneity at the subnanogram level. When PLDS20 is applied to a representative HPC5000 (8000 ppm) library, it distinguishes four subpopulation clusters (A, B, C and D) in which its predicted enrichment for subpopulation membership was too low to be statistically significant ( p = 0.11). By contrast, using a representative MPL library<sup>2</sup> that is over 1000 ppm more soluble, PLDS20 clustered into five subpopulation groups (A, B, C, D and E). Although the models were unable to predict binding affinity in terms of scores; the pattern of assignment of highest enrichment was similar for all five of the HPC5000 solutions (ranging from 0.70 to 0.86); for the MPL libraries, the annotations were only obtained for two non-monotonic groups (D and E). While only one model provided higher predictions than the others in terms of enrichment, as expected, it assigned the same assignments as the others, including population B. However, even at these subpopulation levels, PLDS20 still exhibits strong divergence across the subpopulation boundaries. Despite some shortfalls and inconsistencies, PLDS20 is a simple-to-use tool, with some notable findings, for benchmarking and interpretation of sub-population (sub-nanogram) classifications to non-monotonic phenomenon.

Scintillation quantum dots (SQDs) are fascinating nano-constructs with an intriguing structure-property relationship. The interaction between dye monomers and excitation can directly affect the size of the quantum dots, but the reasons for their interaction have not been fully clarified. Based on the adaptive dipole of nearby resonance, we propose that SDOs can directly assemble the resonant electronic ground state (RGSS) of dye monomers at the interface of adjacent solvent molecules. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we show that this process allows the efficient use of SQD materials with a single dye monomer. First, we confirm the origin of the interface property through DFT and show that a sequence of ROS containing dyes absorbs at wavelengths of 610 nm and 750 nm. Second, we show that the interface properties are maintained when changing the dye composition, which further supports our insight that the interface is non-specific. Third, the result of this approach can improve the detection sensitivity of the SQD probes, which are widely used in the research of IR fluorescence and optical detection. In summary, this work highlights the first cross-functional interface property that directly links the exciton energy landscape with the response of an interface. Such interface results that link the excitation with the interface, without a third physical layer, have important research implications in the development of photonic devices, logic, and signal processing.

Author SummaryWith the advent of quantum information technologies, sensing at the nanoscale has attracted significant interest. In the context of solid-state semiconductors, many different semiconducting QD molecular complexes have been reported. Some of these complexes are used as photonic qubits and modulators, and thus have become a focus of intense research. Nevertheless, with the increased complexity of QD systems, there are emerging concerns over the stability and scalability of existing systems. In this work, we have identified a family of nanocrystals where the bulk of the dye molecules are located on the surface and interface with the solvent molecules. With a surface and interface size of about 300 nm in diameter, and short distance-dependent dipole interactions, the absorption peak of various molecules is effectively tuned to a wavelength around 630 nm, which is both the absorption peak and the second-resonance peak of a photochromic dye. This allows us to effectively detect a portion of these molecules on the surface and reduce the cost of fabrication. Our results illustrate a direct connection between the excitonic energy landscape of molecules and the interface response of their colloidal assemblies, which has implications for the optimization and use of QD materials

Lightweight fluorescent molecular sensors can monitor single molecules with nanoscale resolution in real time. A powerful strategy to develop novel molecular probes is to design highly diverse chemical probes based on metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) in-situ functionalized on a solid support. In particular, the Selectolate MOF was the first and only 1D ligand in an I-VI series of oligomeric cations, composed of oxodithiolate oligomers, which give well defined fluorescence arising from chromophores that exhibit very different optical activities (electronic dipole transitions). Despite having the same electronegativity (δ=-1.3 and 0.5 relative to pyridine), each triplatinate ion has different excited state vibrationally selective electronic transitions. This expansion of the Optritine family of fluorescent molecules provides a major advance in the synthetic toolbox of molecular sensors in which several sensing combinations were generated for the first time in the room-temperature range. We show here that large variations in UV wavelength, photosensitivity and multico-functionalization can be achieved and that optical activity is essential in design and tuning the activity of this family of molecular probes.

Highlights
  -Selectolate I-VI series of oxodithiolate oligomers were designed from a 1D mZn[3]pn[2]Tlan ligand with design in 2D symmetry.
  -Highly tunable bandgaps and resonances were achieved: 3.3 nm from ground state to 1.0 eV, both modulated by the type of bridging oxotrianion unit.
  -Tuning of enhanced multico-functionalization is reported: strong fluorescence emitted by oxato-redox, mutasynergistic and muta-antipyrene.
  -Optical activity of the receptor ions were reported in a wide range: >2 eV per oxo-nitrile proton pair, and up to 6.05 eV per solvent-proton pair.
  -Surface-sensitive systems can be imaged in-situ on a mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) by spin-labeling.

Electromagnetism is a cornerstone of the dynamic behavior of organic systems. Despite the remarkable synthesis capabilities of supramolecular organic chemistry, recent computational studies have revealed the limited ability of molecular machines to detect changes in electromagnetic field. These limitations stem from the inherent complexity of the system, a consequence of the large number of modes in organic semiconductors, the overrepresentation of electronic modes, and their inherent structural entanglements. Our manuscript integrates an open-source DNA reporter toolkit designed for cooperative operation with large-scale quantum simulations of molecular systems to investigate the influence of electromagnetic coupling on molecular machines. The approach permits a tight control over the local environment of organic conductors. We demonstrate the ability to rotate and selectively transport chromophores using external laser light and probe the electrostatic field directly by probing the optical transitions at specific resonance wavelengths. We further demonstrate a second-order gate state of organic semiconductor by extending the excitation laser to tune a direct state and demonstrate the capability of this system to implement quantum gates with zero gate error and outperform molecular logic gates by orders of magnitude.

Compact high-efficiency, high-affinity, perchlorate-based optical fluorescence sensors present a revolutionary paradigm for water monitoring and purification, mitigating underpowered analyses and cost-efficiency in existing detection methodologies. Here, we present a groundbreaking sensor, designed to operate under 1 V O_Z_DQ_C, with a 1 mM sodium perchlorate reference standard and a 437-nm excitation light. This cutting-edge sensor, characterized via comparison with state-of-the-art OptiSensor standards (Mesa, California), a portable, handheld instrument, and the Microsoft MVP Green Energy app, exhibited an exceptionally high internal quantum efficiency (IAQ) of 94.24%, showcasing superior sensitivity and selectivity compared to standard sensors. This sensor is meticulously designed for user-friendliness, with parameters configurable via the Green Energy user app for uncomplicated operating guidelines. Epoxy paraphenylamine is an organic fluorophore that displays a broad emission band (544 nm) that transitions from a UV-blue peak in the dark state to a green-yellow emission in the light state. Beyond the standard lifetimes observed in the visible range, multiphoton lifetimes (3.5 ms) within this label are believed to be unique to this fluorophore. We explored the lifetimes by monitoring samples from multiple copies and single molecules (through all molecular states of excitation), and reported that the emission lifetimes vary significantly as a function of molecule configurations: Upon forming dimers, dimers usually have longer lifetimes compared to small molecules and triplets, indicating that their lifetimes increase with size of excitation. For molecules with higher Franck-Condon (FC) energy, a different behavior was observed, and triplet lifetimes (max. ~50 ns) were significantly reduced with larger FC energy. Furthermore, it was found that the lifetime distributions of triplet-triplet levels are narrow compared to the sequential sample distribution at low and high FC energy (100-500, 300-800 kJ mol-1), while the sample lifetimes at both energies are similar. These results suggest that short triplet lifetimes are an important phenomenon for dynamic multiphoton fluorescence, and one potential means of employing this change in emission fluorescence lifetime to probe molecular recognition. However, this potential usefulness of lifetime manipulations for multiphoton studies is masked by the poorly controlled environment of biological samples and measured optical parameters.

Palmatine is a protoberberine alkaloid, which may produce singlet oxygen under visible light irradiation and binds to DNA. The fact that singlet oxygen activation in palmatine may be triggered by environmental conditions, and in particular its interaction with nucleic acids, makes it a most suitable candidate for photodynamic therapy and DNA-targeted non-invasive anticancer strategies. Despite these remarkable properties the actual binding mode between palmatine and DNA has not been resolved, yet. Its elucidation has, indeed, led to contrasting hypothesis. In this contribution by using long-range molecular dynamic simulations and enhanced sampling approaches, we unequivocally identify that intercalation is the dominant binding mode of palmatine with DNA, from either a thermodynamic and kinetic point of view.

Glucose sensing is vital for managing diabetes. However, current sensors are invasive and secrete enzymatic byproducts that are inflammatory and toxic. Though DNA-wrapped single-walled carbon nanotubes (DNA-SWCNTs) emit fluorescence that is ideal for enzyme-free optical sensing, existing approaches have yet to identify a DNA sequence that can elicit a fluorescence response to glucose. We develop an approach based on clustering to design a diverse library of 90 DNA sequences to screen for a glucose response. The most responsive sequence was further improved based on favorable mutations predicted by deep learning and pattern recognition. This combination of experimental screening and supervised and unsupervised machine learning represents a generalizable approach to developing DNA-SWCNT sensors for even the most elusive analytes.

DNA-based data storage is a promising solution to the challenges of large-scale data storage. However, the low throughput of the mainstream inkjet-based DNA synthesis method has hindered its widespread adoption. In contrast, high-throughput electrochemical synthesis provides higher throughput but with more nucleotide insertion, deletion, and substitution errors. Here, we propose an innovative coding scheme with high error correction capabilities, called DNA StairLoop. This coding scheme features a staircase interleaver and allows for component codes such as the convolutional code and the ow-density Parity-check code, allowing for flexible adaptation of the coding scheme. Both the row and the column decoders are soft input and soft output, enabling further improvement in data recovery accuracy through iterative decoding. The staircase interleaver facilitates extensive parallel decoding capabilities while effectively preserving parallelism across a multitude of nodes. In the in vitro experiment, DNA StairLoop successfully recovered the raw information in a staircase block with a nucleotide error rate of more than 8%. The simulations revealed that the DNA StairLoop can correct 10% nucleotide errors. Moreover, in parallel computing processing, the decoding time of our code continues to decrease dramatically.

Nitrogen-vacancy centers in nanodiamonds exhibit photo-stability and biocompatibility that make them promising candidates for versatile biological sensors. In the present work, we study the dependence of NV-nanodiamond fluorescence on the pH of the surrounding ionic aqueous solution. Band-bending effects and modified ion migration rates may be the potential mechanisms underlying the observed pH sensitivity. Our work offers insight into diamond electrochemistry and paves the way toward nanoscale pH imaging. Additionally, the methodologies developed in this work introduce a viable approach for analyzing local electrochemical environments, with potential applications in intra-cellular pH sensing, the design of electrolytic cells, and the development of alternative fuel technologies.

A novel and ubiquitous approach to detecting and monitoring infectious disease outbreaks is through artificial intelligence (AI). Research indicates AI can assist with disease prevention and treatment at scale and improved surveillance and early warning for COVID-19 has been performed through data analytics. However, many criteria considered in disease surveillance for infectious disease outbreaks do not map directly to AI indicators. This study provides a framework to explain these criteria and help inform AI applications. Using one rule-based test for identifying outbreaks from administrative data, the study compares disease detection AI indicators to their corresponding criteria across 19 global territories and 200 healthcare facilities in Europe. Decision curves were generated for each rule using a normalization method to simulate predictive power. Results indicate that screening methods using weighted entropy closely match many of the criteria for health warnings, though some such as confirmed cases and any new cases are missed. We propose a rule to detect diseases in the 200 tested healthcare facilities and propose a hybrid approach to using rule-based testing through rule similarity, rule-based testing, and auditing. The research supports the importance of mapping criteria to AI indicators to enable the most effective use of AI for infectious disease outbreak monitoring.
