Pandemic Influenza may be a costlier affair, especially for a newly configured state with scarce Human Resources. There is an urgent need to provide flexibility in response to multi-faceted emergencies like COVID-19, influenza, and any infectious disease outbreaks. However, such flexibility is time-consuming to operationalize using traditional forecasting techniques. Here, we extend traditional Forecasting methods with causal Temporal (t) Neural Networks to achieve near-real-time seasonal prediction for essential services and notify them to the leaders based on their duty cycles. These tNNs employ phylogenetic inference of disease dynamics as inputs, identify correlated peaks and long-term trends, and forecast. Three different biological datasets are used to illustrate the modeling capabilities of our proposed tNNs, the first dataset utilizes a small sample size(n=100), the second dataset uses a medium sample size(n=200), and the third dataset uses a large sample size(n=1000). We show that seasonal forecasts produced by our proposed tNNs outperform existing forecasting methods on every disease in terms of time, cost, and effort expended. Our long-term and trajectory forecasts can be shared among federal and state governments, to generate pre-pandemic and pandemic scenario reports from real-time data.

In viral pandemic situations, individuals may choose to forego hygienic behaviors like handwashing and mitigate the risks of their interactions with others due to health-related costs. However, there is evidence that individuals do not abide by such behavior when someone outside the group nearby, also known as the dispersed edge effects. Hence, it remains an open question how those arise and are mitigated, and whether such coping strategies can help the patients with future viral outbreaks. Here, we propose that mitigated practices of prevention may ultimately undermine the collective utility and increase the risk of disease transmission as a consequence of evolutionary supercooperation. We use a computational model and simulated data to conduct a time-series analysis in the presence of various infection suppression strategies and demonstrate that the supercooperative equilibrium as a consequence of mitigation leads to a higher level of disease transmission. Moreover, the evolutionary approach elucidates the underlying causes of mitigation as a consequence of decreasing personal benefits from contagion and strengthens the rationale of similar social-benign strategies as proposed by other scholars. Our results underscore the potential of mitigating behavior to undermine the collective welfare and caution that pre-pandemic cultural shifts, despite their purported improvement, may not always contribute to a rise in collective health.

Financial behaviour research in developing countries is dominated by high-income data in development. Moreover, public health and economic data are generally under-reported in low- and middle-income countries, and are rarely linked across these data. In response, we present a systematic three-step framework for linking public health and economic data to address resource gaps in academic-practice models of low- and middle-income countries, thereby augmenting the capacity of low- and middle-income countries to diagnose priorities and suggest policy alternatives to improve maternal and child health and school readiness in low- and middle-income countries. While still nascent, this approach allows researchers to systematically test model assumptions and harness the power of synthetic data.

COVID-19 transmission is dependent on infection rates across population groups. However, the impact of the level of population immunity on transmission, as well as the features of natural immunity, has not been explored in detail. We assessed the natural immunity of U.S. adults (18-90 years) to the 2020-2021 U.S. coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, including diversity and several measures of natural infection protection across the population. We utilized historical and pandemic network data to investigate the association of immunity factors with disease prevalence and the severity of the initial pandemic wave. We estimated the time course of protective natural immunity to inform design of vaccination programs.

Geographic locations were used to partition population immunity into primary (0-3 months) and secondary (3-6 months) measurements across 18-90 year-olds. Survival in the first 3 months of the pandemic differed substantially by geographic location, with the highest percent mortality at mid-March 2020, which suggests rapid immune decline as the percentage of adults who were already infected grew over the epidemic period.

Secondary infections were less frequent in locations with lower vaccination coverage. Both higher levels of vaccine uptake and higher immunity (as measured by a measure of vaccine-induced antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus spike protein) at the onset of the pandemic were associated with lower disease incidence, although a vaccine-induced increase in antibodies induced by 2021 COVID-19 was not associated with lower transmission. Vaccination had the greatest impact on increasing vaccine coverage (and secondarily on decreasing the rate of waning of vaccinated immunity).

Temporal association analyses revealed that circulating mutations, and not vaccine type, was the biggest risk factor for inefficacy of either sequence-based or vaccine-induced immunity. The most effective sequence-based and vaccine-induced immunity against the aforementioned COVID-19 subvariants H1.6 (B.1.617.2) and BA.1 of B.1.1.7 (Beta) variants were the most significant.

These findings suggest that natural immunity, not vaccines, is an important consideration in future COVID-19 prevention strategies. The identification of mechanisms mediating infection protection enables future improvements in disease mitigation strategies, including vaccination and infection prevention.

Computational models have matured to the point where they can begin to generate comprehensive predictions on the health and economic impacts of a major pandemic, such as COVID-19. The National Institutes of Health Clinical and Translation Science (CTSI) is a recently launched National Institutes of Health (NIH) program designed to support large-scale computational modeling of COVID-19 and other infectious diseases. This model is modelled after CTSI programming models from other NIH, such as the Influenza Pandemic Planning Model (IPPM), and the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) Distributed Computation Project (DCP), by addressing high-level, comprehensive forecasting of COVID-19 impacts based on four levers of health: PCR/Pathology, Immunity, Vaccines, and Infection. To create a more complete and robust computational model of COVID-19, we optimized the GCP, a previously published multimodal parameterization scheme used for all of the CTSI. In this manuscript, we describe the primary features of GCP (including all 4 models currently planned for including in the human body, respiratory virus genome, and antibody, as well as respiratory virus genome evolution), our results during extensive parameter tuning, and plan to include additional features for future output refinement. We introduce our modeling concepts and explain how the GCP is developed and extended.

HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), particularly pre-exposure prophylaxis combined with medication (Pre-PCO), is the standard approach to preventing HIV infections in high-risk populations. However, in part due to lack of knowledge about the benefit and effectiveness of other preventive interventions, interventions that are cost-effective, widely acceptable, and practical to use are lacking. To this end, we experimentally tested the effects of two types of low-dose pre-exposure prophylaxis: 450 (iPrEx 450) and 750 (iPrEx 750), alongside a non-pharmacological strategy to prevent HIV infection that uses  simulated culinary ingredients such as shrimp, wine, and curry powder. All interventions were tested against an earlier HIV exposure in 59 HIV-negative participants (mean 4.27 years) prior to beginning the intervention. Compared to a placebo, iPrEx 750 significantly reduced the 1-year incidence of HIV after an HIV exposure of more than two years, and the benefit was significantly greater with 750 than with 450. Importantly, both interventions were comparable in effectiveness when used as monotherapy as compared to a lower dosage of HIV prevention strategy. There were no significant difference in the effects of these interventions compared to those of behavioral treatments. Among a small sample size and the long temporal dimension of HIV infection in this study, our results provide further evidence that strategies which prevent HIV infection through enhanced immunity can prevent the progression of disease, suggesting a potential role for them among vulnerable populations.

Long and variable infectious diseases have a profound influence on human behavior. Such infectious diseases are continually shaped by the social dynamics, policies and beliefs that individuals have regarding the disease. The last few years have witnessed a rise in interest in the intersection of disease and politics, motivated by a growing evidence base on the powerful effects that political decisions, social norms and individual behavior have on infectious disease outcomes. However, our understanding of the political, institutional and economic factors that influence infectious disease behavior remains limited. To address this, we first develop a comprehensive risk and behavioral approach that predicts a pandemic with the most severe consequences, incorporating factors such as vaccine diffusion, economic disparity and social norms to influence individual risk perceptions, disease behavior and public responses. Our findings highlight the critical importance of these factors, especially the influence of public attitudes towards infectious diseases, their cognitive side effects and individual beliefs. Our study presents a holistic picture of political, social and economic dynamics that influence individual behavior and risk perception, shedding light on the interplay between individuals and society in disease response and management.

Author SummaryUnderstanding the factors that lead to the emergence, transmission, and impact of an infectious disease is crucial for improving individual health and national policy decisions. In this study, we propose a new framework that takes into account human behavioral dynamics and political and economic trends in disease response. Our work reveals the essential role that both factors play, through which individual behaviors, social norms, and public opinion can significantly impact disease control and health outcomes. We also highlight the critical importance of understanding the dynamics of behavioral choices and political impacts. From the paper written by Elizabeth M Zeilig

The Covid-19 pandemic exposed many limitations of the generic medicine sector: uneven access to diagnostic tools, poor hospital capacity, missing skills for standardization and quality control. Fast containment by a single antiviral agent can blur the differences and strengthen the role of trade negotiators -or, conversely, speed up diversification of drug and device sourcing. A good framework for monitoring and predicting pandemics must rely on big data from hospitals and on real-time data, both in supply chains and in key diseases management. We describe the 3In-MiTooling platform that combines disease modelling (predictive power) with industry intelligence and hospital data in a single, scalable and open-source software stack. We show its application to influenza and other pathogens and to the case of blood supply for Covid-19 (blood component storage and blood component bio-safety in single-use versus transfusion) which will provide clear evidence of the availability of a reliable blood components supply for non-vaccine-derived blood. The 3IN-MiTooling framework allows the integration of real-time hospital data to refine supply prediction. The platform facilitates the adaptive design and feedback of future research and modelling and proves its practical utility in a real-world situation.

A clear bias is that the highest-performing countries in developing its defense capability are likely to have a superior command, control, communications, and computers-cyber (C4C) capability for military operations, combat operations, and information-centric operations. Yet, there is limited evidence from military operational and research literature showing the overall relationship between command, control, communications and computers (C4C), and military operation, combat, and information-centric operations of different countries. For this reason, the objective of this study is to develop a statistical multi-country robustness index by combining the five most widely-used command, control, communications, and computers-cyber (C4C) indicators of three advanced high-capability armed and autonomous military forces (or friendly combatant powers of both world powers) - United States Armed Forces, China Armed Forces, and Russia Armed Forces. This study offers a counterintuitive finding: no bilateral military alliance, conventional army, and/or regional defense alliance between China and Russia and the United States (with the United States as the foremost military partner) has led to a corresponding bilateral C4C capability development for military operations, combat operations, and information-centric operations. Instead, each military alliance appeared to contribute differently to their military operations, combat operations, and information-centric operations based on the development of their capabilities, particularly for coalition military forces formed of such alliances. As a result, the study has drawn two conclusions: First, the perceived influence of the military alliance in the development of a bilateral C4C capability might be lower than is assumed. Secondly, the level of importance of the international military alliance or bilateral military alliance to develop their respective C4C capabilities was non-monotonic and showed a U-shaped curve with respect to increasing military alliances. However, the strongest relationships between the amount of acquisition, development, and usage of long-range precision weapons by China and Russia and their respective C4C capabilities. Therefore, the trend may be that the military alliance among China and Russia during the 2020s, combined with the U.S.-China and U.S.-Russia relations, could put the various Western military alliances into a competition to acquire long-range precision weapons and thus increase their own defense capabilities.

Ambient air pollution has highly adverse effects on public health and the environment, particularly in urban areas of the Global South. Systematic air quality monitoring (AQM) is a precondition for effective policies to mitigate this problem, and making AQM data publicly available also signals commitment to take action. Thus far, little is known about the global capacity for public AQM, and how it varies across geographic location, pollution exposure, and socio-economic characteristics. We thus constructed a novel, geocoded dataset on AQM behavior in more than ten thousand urban areas of low to middle-income countries. In almost 90% of these urban areas, we are unable to identify any monitoring activity, and the form and extent of AQM in the remaining 10% varies greatly. Income levels and characteristics of political institutions (democracy) turn out to be key drivers of variation in AQM activity, with urban areas in more democratic countries more likely to respond with more AQM to high air pollution levels. The evidence provided here can serve as a wake-up call for public authorities, international institutions, and civil society stakeholders to invest far more than hitherto the case into AQM, particularly in under-monitored, less affluent, and less democratic settings.

A major priority for epidemiological research in a time of anthropogenic change is understanding how infectious disease dynamics respond to perturbations. Interventions to slow the spread of SARS-CoV-2 significantly disrupted the transmission of other human pathogens. As interventions lifted, whether and when respiratory pathogens would eventually return to their pre-pandemic dynamics remains to be answered. Here, we present a framework for estimating pathogen resilience based on how fast epidemic patterns approach their pre-pandemic, endemic dynamics and analyze relevant time series data from Hong Kong, Canada, Korea, and the US. By quantifying the resilience of common respiratory pathogens, we are able to predict when each pathogen will eventually return to its pre-pandemic dynamics. Our predictions closely match the observed deviations (or lack thereof) from the pre-COVID dynamics of respiratory pathogens. Discrepancies between predicted and observed dynamics indicate the long-term impacts of pandemic perturbations, suggesting that some pathogens may be converging to a different endemic cycle. Finally, we show that the replenishment rate of the susceptible population is a key determinant of pathogen resilience, which in turn determines the sensitivity of a system to stochastic perturbations. Overall, our analysis highlights the persistent nature of common respiratory pathogens compared to vaccine-preventable infections, such as measles.

Zoonotic diseases have received significantly more attention over the last few decades, emerging with increasing frequency and causing the majority of notable disease outbreaks in this century, including the COVID-19 pandemic. As human activities and shifting climate patterns induce changes in the environment that alter habitat and range of reservoir species, the potential for human and animal interactions will increase and enhance the opportunity for spillover. Thus, any emergency response preparedness planning must take into account the function and coordination of agencies across the sectors of human, animal and environmental health. Within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania a table-top exercise was performed to evaluate a multi-agency response during a hypothetical zoonotic disease investigation. The exercise was evaluated by the participants to gain feedback on the overall process and lessons learned. Here, we describe the tabletop exercise scenario and the insights gained. We found that differences in operational structure create challenges for interdepartmental communication and in the ability to resource a coordinated response, highlighting opportunities to develop infrastructure that will facilitate future actions. A set of recommendations are outlined that may enhance cross-agency activities and promote more effective and efficient emergency response.

BackgroundIn Cote dIvoire, Aedes vector studies and arboviral outbreak responses have mostly focused on urbanized neighborhoods including intra-urban villages, but have often neglected peripheral villages. We assessed and compared Aedes aegypti population dynamics and dengue (DEN) and yellow fever (YF) epidemic risks among peri-urban and intra-urban villages during the 2023-2024 DEN outbreaks in Cocody-Bingerville, southern Cote dIvoire.

MethodsFrom August 2023 to July 2024, we sampled Aedes eggs, larvae and pupae in the domestic and peridomestic ecozones of three peri-urban and three intra-urban villages. We compared Ae. aegypti larval infestation, container productivity, Stegomyia indices (house index: HI, container index: CI, and Breteau index: BI) and pupal indices (pupae per house index: PHI, pupae per container index: PCI, and pupae per person index: PPI) between the study villages.

ResultsAedes aegypti widely dominated Aedes fauna in both peri-urban (98.1%) and intra-urban (99.8%) villages. Immatures were sampled from seven container types. However, the most productive containers were small containers, tires and medium containers which produced 81.8% of all the pupae in the peri-urban villages, and tires and small containers yielding 83.2% in the intra-urban villages. These key containers produced substantially more pupae in the domestic ecozones (70.9%) in the peri-urban villages, but equitably between the domestic (48.8%) and peridomestic (51.2%) ecozones in the intra-urban villages. In each study village, they yielded around 90% and 80% of pupae during the short dry and long rainy seasons, respectively. CI, HI and BI were comparable between the peri-urban (29.9%, 35.9% and 41.4) and intra-urban (36.7%, 48.0% and 56.2) villages, and surpassed the World Health Organization (WHO) DEN and YF epidemic thresholds. PCI (1.26 vs. 3.38 pupae/container) and PHI (1.75 vs. 5.18 pupae/house) were lower in the peri-urban than in the intra-urban villages, while PPI (0.54 vs. 1.25 pupae/person) was similar between the villages. Unlike temperature and relative humidity, all indices were strongly associated with rainfall in all the study villages.

ConclusionIn Cocody-Bingerville, all sampled peri-urban and intra-urban villages exhibited high densities of Ae. aegypti immatures and habitats. Although larval habitats were diverse, a limited number of container types accounted for over 80% of pupal production. Stegomyia indices remained consistently elevated, exceeding WHO epidemic thresholds for DEN and YF across all study villages, potentially contributing to ongoing DEN outbreaks. Therefore, vector surveillance and outbreak responses should be extended to peri-urban villages, as they could act as arbovirus re-introduction sources. Community-based interventions targeting the identified key containers could help control the outbreaks. This study provides a baseline for strategically reducing human exposure to arboviruses in the study villages.

sample_q_texts: Clustering can be used to detect cell clusters in 3D imaging data, but the underlying process of clustering is poorly understood. To quantify, localize, and understand the mechanism of clustering in a bioinformatic workflow, we developed a workflow, called Trio_Task, that leverages a mixture of clustering methods, aimed at performing high-throughput clustering in arbitrary spatial orientations, by combining free matching and consistent alignment. We successfully applied the methodology to 3D mass-spectrometry imaging datasets from human and mouse primary lung tissues, demonstrating that cluster-based analysis is a crucial component in enhancing knowledge from high-resolution spatially-resolved mass-spectrometry imaging experiments, and also helps to identify cell types and cell clusters. We believe this work can serve as a benchmark against which to develop a reproducible and robust spatial clustering method for high-throughput 3D mass-spectrometry imaging experiments.
sample_p_texts: Spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT) and spatially resolved proteomics (SRP) data enable the study of gene expression and protein abundances within their precise spatial and cellular contexts in tissues. Certain SRT and SRP tech-nologies also capture corresponding morphology images, adding another layer of valuable information. However, few existing methods developed for SRT data effectively leverage these supplementary images to enhance clustering performance. Here, we introduce stDyer-image, an end-to-end deep learning framework designed for clustering for SRT and SRP datasets with images. Unlike existing methods that utilize images to complement gene expression data, stDyer-image directly links image features to cluster labels. This approach draws inspiration from pathologists, who can visually identify specific cell types or tumor regions from morphological images without relying on gene expression or protein abundances. Benchmarks against state-of-the-art tools demonstrate that stDyer-image achieves superior performance in clustering. Moreover, it is capable of handling large-scale datasets across diverse technologies, making it a versatile and powerful tool for spatial omics analysis.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has shown remarkable promise in pathology applications, shedding light on the spatial organization of gene expression and its relationship to the tumor microenvironment. However, its clinical adoption remains constrained due to the limited scalability of current sequencing technologies. While recent methods attempt to infer ST from whole slide images (WSIs) using pretrained image encoders, they remain restricted by limited gene coverage, organ-specific training, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning. In light of this, we introduce STPath, a generative foundation model pretrained on a large-scale collection of WSIs paired with ST profiles. This extensive pretraining enables STPath to directly predict gene expression across 38,984 genes and 17 organs without requiring downstream fine-tuning. STPath integrates multiple data modalities, including histological images, gene expressions, organ type, and sequencing technology information, within a novel geometry-aware Transformer architecture. Unlike previous methods that directly map WSIs to gene expression, STPath is trained using a masked gene expression prediction objective guided by tailored noise schedules, effectively balancing between capturing gene-gene dependencies and performing high-quality predictions. We evaluate STPath across 6 tasks spanning 23 datasets and 14 biomarkers, including gene expression prediction, spot imputation, spatial clustering, biomarker prediction, gene mutation prediction, and survival prediction. These results demonstrate STPaths strong ability to infer spatially resolved gene expression and reveal crucial pathological structures within tissue samples, underscoring its promise for scalable ST-based pathology applications.

State-of-the-art spatial proteomic and transcriptomic technologies can deeply pheno-type cells in their native tissue environment, providing a high throughput means to effectively quantify spatial relationships between diverse cell populations. However, the experimental design choice of which regions of a tissue will be imaged can greatly impact the interpretation of spatial quantifications. That is, spatial relationships identified in one region of interest may not be interpreted consistently across other regions. To address this challenge, we introduce Kontextual, a method which considers alternative frames of reference for contextualising spatial relationships. These contexts may represent landmarks, spatial domains, or groups of functionally similar cells which are consistent across regions. By modelling spatial relationships between cells relative to these contexts, Kontextual produces robust spatial quantifications that are not confounded by the region selected. We demonstrate in spatial proteomics and spatial transcriptomics datasets that modelling spatial relationships this way is biologically meaningful. We also demonstrate how this approach can be used in a classification setting to improve prediction of patient prognosis.

Advances in spatial profiling have resulted in the generation of multi-omic atlases that span biological scales. In general, multiple workflows are required for image registration, coordinate registration, and spot deconvolution to integrate modalities. To improve the throughput of registration of multi-omic cohorts, we introduce PIVOT, a user-friendly and open-source interface for streamlined nonlinear registration. We demonstrate PIVOTs strengths through registration of three multi-omic datasets, and show comparison of its performance to existing workflows.

The generation of spatial data in biology has been transformed by multiplex imaging and spatial-omics technologies, such as single cell spatial transcriptomics. These approaches permit a detailed mapping of cell populations and phenotypes within the tissue context, which reveals that tissues are complex ecosystems that include multiple organisational structures over different length scales. Quantitative methods for maximising the information that can be retrieved from these images have not kept pace with technological advances in platforms, and no standard methodology has emerged for spatial data analysis. Proposed pipelines are often tailored to individual studies, leading to a fragmented landscape of available methods, and no clear guidance about which statistical tools are best suited to a particular research question.

In response to these challenges, we present MuSpAn, a Multiscale Spatial Analysis package designed to provide straightforward access to well-established and cutting-edge mathematical tools for analysing spatial data. MuSpAn provides easy to use, flexible, and interactive access to quantitative methods developed from mathematical fields that include spatial statistics, topological data analysis, network theory, geometry, probability and ecology. Users can construct custom pipelines from tools across these fields to address specific biological problems, or conduct unbiased exploration of data for discovery spatial biology. In summary, MuSpAn is an extensive platform which enables multiscale analysis of spatial data, ranging from the subcellular to the tissue-scale.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have revolutionized tissue architecture studies by capturing gene expression with spatial context. However, high-dimensional ST data often have limited spatial resolution and exhibit considerable noise and sparsity, posing significant challenges in deciphering subtle spatial structures and underlying biological activities. Here, we introduce SpaHDmap, an interpretable dimension reduction framework that enhances spatial resolution by integrating ST gene expression with high-resolution histology images. SpaHDmap incorporates non-negative matrix factorization into a multimodal fusion encoder-decoder architecture, enabling the identification of interpretable, high-resolution embeddings. Furthermore, SpaHDmap can simultaneously analyze multiple samples and is compatible with various types of histology images. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real ST datasets from various technologies and tissue types demonstrate that SpaHDmap can effectively produce highly interpretable, high-resolution embeddings, and detects refined spatial structures. SpaHDmap represents a powerful approach for integrating ST data and histology images, offering deeper insights into complex tissue structures and functions.

Spatially resolved omics (SRO) technologies enable the identification of cell types while preserving their organization within tissues. Application of such technologies offers the opportunity to delineate cell-type spatial relationships, particularly across different length scales, and enhance our understanding of tissue organization and function. To quantify such multi-scale cell-type spatial relationships, we developed CRAWDAD, Cell-type Relationship Analysis Workflow Done Across Distances, as an open-source R package with source code and additional documentation at https://jef.works/CRAWDAD/.

To demonstrate the utility of such multi-scale characterization, recapitulate expected cell-type spatial relationships, and evaluate against other cell-type spatial analyses, we applied CRAWDAD to various simulated and real SRO datasets of diverse tissues assayed by diverse SRO technologies. We further demonstrate how such multi-scale characterization enabled by CRAWDAD can be used to compare cell-type spatial relationships across multiple samples. Finally, we applied CRAWDAD to SRO datasets of the human spleen to identify consistent as well as patient and sample-specific cell-type spatial relationships. In general, we anticipate such multi-scale analysis of SRO data enabled by CRAWDAD will provide useful quantitative metrics to facilitate the identification, characterization, and comparison of cell-type spatial relationships across axes of interest.

We developed an integrated imaging pipeline for spatio-molecular and immunophenotypic tissue analysis, enabling the discovery of molecular markers across spatial scales--from functional tissue units to cell types and neighborhoods. Our approach facilitates single-tissue section analysis, enabling direct cross-modality mining of imaging mass spectrometry and highly multiplexed immunofluorescence microscopy. Demonstrated on human kidney tissue, we identified lipidomic markers of cellular neighborhoods associated with renal cell types and immune cell infiltration.

An important task in the analysis of spatially resolved transcriptomics data is to identify spatially variable genes (SVGs), or genes that vary in a 2D space. Current approaches rank SVGs based on either p-values or an effect size, such as the proportion of spatial variance. However, previous work in the analysis of RNA-sequencing identified a technical bias, referred to as the "mean-variance relationship", where highly expressed genes are more likely to have a higher variance. Here, we demonstrate the mean-variance relationship in spatial transcriptomics data. Furthermore, we propose spoon, a statistical framework using Empirical Bayes techniques to remove this bias, leading to more accurate prioritization of SVGs. We demonstrate the performance of spoon in both simulated and real spatial transcriptomics data. A software implementation of our method is available at https://bioconductor.org/packages/spoon.

Spatial transcriptomics is advancing molecular biology by providing high-resolution insights into gene expression within the spatial context of tissues. This context is essential for identifying spatial domains, enabling the understanding of micro-environment organizations and their implications for tissue function and disease progression. To improve current model limitations on multiple slides, we have designed Novae (https://github.com/MICS-Lab/novae), a graph-based foundation model that extracts representations of cells within their spatial contexts. Our model was trained on a large dataset of nearly 30 million cells across 18 tissues, allowing Novae to perform zero-shot domain inference across multiple gene panels, tissues, and technologies. Unlike other models, it also natively corrects batch effects and constructs a nested hierarchy of spatial domains. Furthermore, Novae supports various downstream tasks, including spatially variable gene or pathway analysis and spatial domain trajectory analysis. Overall, Novae provides a robust and versatile tool for advancing spatial transcriptomics and its applications in biomedical research.

Functional diversity in the fungus Neocallimastix mesenteroides is considered the most diverse and genetically most complex described fungal genus for soil fungi, with species occupying vast ecological niches throughout the continental United States and beyond. Despite intensive cultivation and sequencing techniques, taxonomic diversity remains elusive. Further, the diversity within the lineage of species is unclear, as few karyotypes have been published. Here, we mapped karyotype and genome-wide SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) data for Neocallimastix. We demonstrate that nuclear karyotype variability is consistent with a tetraploid (2n = 8) organization, with 165 kb of differential chromosome length between ploidy levels. This is the first genome-wide-SNP reference for Neocallimastix mesenteroides and represents a critical update to prior studies. Additionally, we compare Neocallimastix to Clavicia ibida and identify a previously unknown synonym of Clavicia. Additionally, we uncover several basic, pleiotropic variants in the genome of Neocallimastix for genome-wide expansion of tax domains. Overall, our work represents a strong attempt to increase genomic biodiversity and the taxonomic completeness of Neocallimastix mesenteroides by identifying species that have not been identified through manual or automated systems for over a century.

Critical perspectives are essential for understanding a wide range of systems, but this requires multidisciplinary perspectives and expertise in the language of science. To address the growing need for critical perspectives in life science research in the future, we have revised, upgraded, and redeveloped the Critical Perspectives in Genomics (CPG) Language and Primer (CPL) Scheme to provide a standardized framework for critical perspectives in genomics. We present our vision and outline the revised, improved CPL Scheme, providing a detailed description and examples. We seek input on the language and its application in genomics from the community before finalizing the scheme. We have expanded the functionality of the CPPLT to include a comprehensive set of 43 criteria for critical perspectives. The criteria, including an expansion of three parameters from 16 to 19, can now be assigned to a variable of the CPPLT and allow more detailed application of the CPG Scheme, allowing for deeper analysis. We present an exhaustive exploration of the criteria, offering a unique perspective on the genetic significance of each criterion in the genomic landscape and progress from the context of genetic landscapes. Overall, we present a clear and standardized language of genomics that fosters systematic critical perspectives for more accurate insights in genomic studies.

Nuclear multigene families are functionally linked within specific cell populations that create variation, however large segments often encompass multiple gene copies, either inherited or through duplication. This raises the question of how such segments came to exist, and what adaptive value they may have possessed in the past. Previous works found that some nucleolar genes conserved only within a eukaryotic nuclear ancestor and have mutated into multiple copies in all modern lineages. We generated nucleolar RNA expression networks and barcode analyses of 357 protein and miRNA targets of seven mitochondrial protein families (mitophotomes and cytochrome c oxidase I and II), to determine whether such pathways exist in-species, of ancient diverged ancestors or both. We used quantitative transcriptomics to characterize patterns of mitochondrial gene expression across multiple species, and corresponding barcode analysis to determine whether nuclear genome expansion and duplication was conserved in the evolution of nuclear evolution and its progenitor. We found abundant mitochondrial gene duplication in the protist eukaryote nuclear ancestor and all extant eukaryotes. We mapped genes that were under evolved nuclear selective pressures and used functional mapping to determine if conserved sequences are inherited from past species. We mapped nuclear ribosomal gene expansion and duplication in protists, early eukaryotes and life domains with and without nuclear dispersal. The relative conservatism of such expansion and duplication increases with eukaryotic phylogenetic time, suggesting continued storage and replication of the ancestral rDNA strategy, but also highlights that conserved proteomic signatures also existed in these groups, likely reflecting modular gene interactions within the shared nuclear genome of protists.

The existence of versatile genetic elements, such as transposons and insertions-deletions, has historically spurred debates about the emergence of modular organizations in mobile elements and the evolution of transposons. Here, we investigate the genomic evolution and transposable element (TE) spread through a systematic analysis of artificial datasets containing both representative and diverse TE elements, as well as repetitive regions like Alu elements. We observe that repetitive regions can serve as genomic intermediates and accelerate TE migration, as evidenced by a more pronounced Te spread. In particular, a coevolutionary link between Alu elements and TE moves is observed, possibly responsible for Te spread during early evolution. Our findings suggest that repetitive regions not only act as genetic anchors but also expedite TE movement in the early stages of evolution. Further, TE spread accelerates as repetitive regions extend their spans. Our analysis suggests that repetitive regions can simultaneously contribute to the analysis of TE evolution and chromosomal organization while acting as architectural structures influencing evolution.

BackgroundDifferential restoration of eukaryotic DNA and RNA libraries in Arabidopsis protoplasts is hampered by inaccuracies in the split and recovery processes, leading to partial and full recovery of only a fraction of the original genomic DNA. We used deep pan-genome sequencing across early-leaf Arabidopsis shoot apoplasts to measure the source of the polymorphism in clonally distributed target gene expression, without RNA preparations and without needing to parse heterochromatic DNA regions, in order to better understand the heterogeneity of Y chromosome function, both in particular chromosomal populations and within the genome.

ResultsY chromosome genomes from 44 insect-compatible A. thaliana cultivars were sequenced across numerous tissues to produce ~32-M total contigs and ~136M highly variant genes (i.e. enhanced levels of polymorphic single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across taxa and tissue type), which were then grouped into multiple gene families based on their shared signatures of subfunctionalization. New alleles arising from specific deletions or duplications were annotated across the pan-genomes, providing insight into the specific roles of each de novo acquired population allele, even if they share the same target gene. We mapped key functions across this gene functional diversity, and we identified additional changes in gene function and duplication rate as a result of the accumulated genetic diversity.

ConclusionsThis study demonstrates the utility of pan-genome sequencing in understanding transcriptional variation in Y chromosome-specific functions, thereby linking and identifying essential genes in the autoinflammatory pathway and steroid hormone metabolism for the progeny of insect-compatible cultivars. This study provides a detailed analysis of population heterogeneity at the genomic level and links transcriptional variation to enzyme-specific polyploidization that is likely to impact both plant evolution and metabolic and genome engineering applications.

The allopolyploid wheat (Hordeum vulgare L.) D2 is an agronomic model crop widely used as a genetic resource for studying species interactions and the biogenesis of apoplastic components of wheat. The genome of the D2 derivative is not available, and a large number of D2 wheat mutants have been discovered recently. Although the cloned reference genome and nucleotide sequence for the D2 are available, computational approach to accurately decipher the architecture of the D2 genome remain under-explored, which hinders the understanding of the genetic basis of some of its major traits. To address this issue, here we present the development of an integrative and flexible computational pipeline for the analysis of the complete reference genome of the D2, as well as the analysis of all its recombinant derivatives, using traditional and state-of-the-art molecular and computational tools for analysis and prediction. These tools include a guided assembly of the D2 genome with an Alissa software pipeline to annotate all protein-encoding coding sequences and all non-protein coding transcripts using the CATH and Uniprot database; a robust prediction of microdeletion candidate sites and a detailed understanding of the genome architecture through the Helindel tool, which maps the regions of the D2 genome encoding protein coding genes to their chromosome positions; and a genome evolutional landscape with leading tools available in CLIMOD analysis. We present an innovative pipeline that assesses the effectiveness of various model-free and method-based approaches, and characterize genotype-phenotype relationships for the genetic diversity and better understand the genetic architecture of this recombinant crop. Our results reveal the genetic diversity, gene duplications, and the relatedness among the recombinant wheat D2. The B-C branch clustering analysis suggests that the D2D2 recombinant phenotype is likely the most derived. A comparative genome analysis of different D2 populations using pathway enrichment and gene expression data generated by the transcriptome-wide expression atlas reveal the crucial role played by the genes of the D2D2 recombination event.

Quantifying and cataloguing variation in biological traits is crucial for understanding their impacts on species fitness. Unfortunately, current tools for high-resolution genetic characterization frequently rely on sequencing or expression data, creating significant challenges for annotating and quantifying variation between species. Here, we describe RegUNsION, a near-native species resolution sequencer-free method that solves this problem by mapping genetic variation in length (GO) and distribution on a single genome simultaneously. We demonstrate its utility by quantitating the regulatory effects of a plant gene across five whole genomes in leaf epidermal cells. The method enables significant improvements over existing methods for extrapolating quantitative trait loci beyond standard GWAS methods, using transcriptomic and epigenomic data, demonstrating its potential for classifying multi-genomic differences across entire species ranges.

The origin of the extreme complexity of bacterial and eukaryotic genomes remains a persistent mystery. Conservation of highly repetitive elements among bacterial and eukaryotic genomes and in ancestral bacterial rRNA encodes signatures of how conserved elements were assembled and recoded during evolution. The diversity of early evolution and RNA evolution have each played important roles in evolution, and they are expected to exert similar effects in evolution of the genome. The simple eukaryotic genome of the blue-green alga Chlamydomonas is a good platform to study the genomic diversification throughout evolution of different repetitive elements. Here, we present genome sequences (NN40686.7_Chla20a.V1.G1) from early-diverging Chloroflexi and their relation to all ancestors of modern eukaryotes in ancestral and derived environmental niches. We show that a single form of chromatin nucleosome remodeling factor H2A.X and the presence of 32 distinct contig segments present in the complex of HRF binding sites in the presence of a ~42-fold retention of an early-diverging chloroplast/plastid fusion is all that is needed for ribosome biogenesis. Our results suggest that a selection process in the ancestral Chloroflexi environment has likely driven the significant diversity and accumulation of specific repetitive elements.
sample_p_texts: Long-read single molecule sequencing technologies continue to grow in popularity for genome assembly and provide an effective way to resolve large and complex genomic variants. However, uptake of these technologies for teaching and training is hampered by the complexity of high molecular weight DNA extraction protocols, the time required for library preparation and the costs for sequencing, as well as challenges with downstream data analyses. Here, we present a full long-read workflow optimised for teaching, that covers each stage from DNA extraction, to library preparation and sequencing, to data QC and genome assembly and characterisation, that can be completed in under two weeks. We use a specific case study of plant identification, where students identify an anonymous plant sample by sequencing and assembling the genome and comparing it to other samples and to reference databases. In testing, long-read genome skimming of nine wild-collected plant species extracted with a modified kit-based approach produced an average of 8Gb of Oxford Nanopore data, enabling the complete assembly of plastid genomes, and partial assembly of nuclear genomes. In the classroom, all students were able to complete the protocols, and to correctly identify their plant samples based on BOLD searches of barcoding loci extracted from the plastid genome, coupled with phylogenetic analyses of whole plastid genomes. We supply all the learning material and raw data allowing this to be adapted to a range of teaching settings.

With the explosive growth of whole-genome datasets, the accurate detection of orthologous synteny has become crucial for the reconstruction of evolutionary history. However, the currently available methods for the identification of orthologous synteny have great limitations: the methods are difficult to scale with varying polyploidy histories, and the accurate removal of out-paralogy is challenging. In this study, we developed a scalable and robust approach, the Orthology Index (OI), to identify orthologous synteny. Our evaluation of a large-scale dataset with diverse polyploidization events demonstrated that the technique is highly reliable. This discovery highlights OI as a potentially unified criterion for the identification of orthologous synteny, and this is further validated using simulation-based benchmarks. In addition, we explore its broad applications in reconstructing the evolutionary histories of plant genomes, including inference of polyploidy, identification of reticulation, and phylogenomics. In conclusion, OI offers a robust, interpretable, and scalable approach for identifying orthologous synteny, significantly enhancing our analytical prowess in plant evolutionary genomics.

Telomeres, the nucleoprotein complexes that protect the ends of linear chromosomes, are essential for maintaining the stability of eukaryotic genomes. As telomeres generally consist of repetitive DNA associated with specifically bound proteins, telomeric repeat motifs (TRMs) are thought to be difficult to evolve. However, a recent study identified nematodes with telomeric repeats distinct from the canonical TTAGGC motif. Here, we investigated how telomere repeats could have evolved despite the challenge posed by the specificity of telomere-binding proteins (TBPs) to the telomeric DNA in Nematoda. We performed a phylogenetic analysis and electrophoresis mobility shift assays to assess the binding affinities of two TBPs, which displayed different conservation patterns. Our results revealed that the well-conserved protein CEH-37 exhibits limited specificity, unable to distinguish telomeric repeats found in nematodes except for the TTAGGG motif, while the less conserved POT proteins displayed rigid specificity. These findings suggest that the emergence of novel telomeric repeat motifs correlated with the characteristics and evolutionary outcomes of TBPs in Nematoda. Our study not only revealed the dynamics of telomere evolution but also enhanced the understanding of the evolutionary relationship between proteins and DNAs.

Lay summaryTelomeres are chromosomal end structures composed of repetitive DNA where telomere-binding proteins (TBPs) specifically bind. This nucleoprotein complex is crucial for eukaryotes to maintain their genome integrity, making it difficult to evolve. However, a recent study identified nematodes with non- canonical telomeric repeat motifs (TRMs). Through an analysis of TBP conservation in Nematoda and assessments of their binding affinities, we observed that the binding capabilities of TBPs align with their conservation patterns. This correlation is also linked to the emergence of novel TRMs, explaining the evolution progress of TRMs in Nematoda. The evolutionary process discovered in this research is not limited to telomeres, providing further insights into evolutionary relationships between proteins and DNA.

Plant mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) experience remarkable levels of horizontal gene transfer (HGT), including the recent discovery that orchids anciently acquired DNA from fungal mitogenomes. Thus far, however, there is no evidence that any of the genes from this interkingdom HGT are functional in orchid mitogenomes. Here, we applied a specialized sequencing approach to the orchid Corallorhiza maculata and found that fungal-derived tRNA genes are transcribed, post-transcriptionally modified, and aminoacylated. In contrast, all the transferred protein-coding sequences appear to be pseudogenes. These findings show that fungal HGT has altered the composition of the orchid mitochondrial tRNA pool and suggest that these foreign tRNAs function in translation. The exceptional capacity of tRNAs for HGT and functional replacement is further illustrated by the diversity of tRNA genes in the C. maculata mitogenome, which also include genes of plastid and bacterial origin in addition to their native mitochondrial counterparts.

Advances in next-generation sequencing technologies over the last decade have substantially reduced the cost and effort required to sequence plant genomes. Whereas early efforts focused primarily on economically important crops and model species, attention has now turned to a broader range of plants, including those with larger and more complex genomes. In 2024, the genomes of 500 plant species were published, including 370 sequenced for the first time. Tracking and providing access to published plant genomes (now covering more than 1800 species) is an invaluable service for plant researchers. PubPlant is an online resource that serves this purpose by cataloging published plant genome sequences and offering multiple visualizations (https://www.plabipd.de/pubplant_main.html). It includes a chronology of genome publications, and cladograms to display the phylogenetic relationships among the sequenced plants. An overview diagram for seed plants highlights taxonomic orders and families with sequenced species, and reveals those that have been overlooked thus far. As a use case for PubPlant, we evaluated the status of sequenced food crops. We found that the five plant families featuring the most food crops were those containing the most sequenced plant species.

Inverted repeats are repetitive elements that can form hairpin and cruciform structures. They are linked to genomic instability, however they also have various biological functions. Their distribution differs markedly across taxonomic groups in the tree of life, and they exhibit high polymorphism due to their inherent genomic instability. Advances in sequencing technologies and declined costs have enabled the generation of an ever-growing number of complete genomes for organisms across taxonomic groups in the tree of life. However, a comprehensive database encompassing inverted repeats across diverse organismal genomes has been lacking. We present InvertiaDB, the first comprehensive database of inverted repeats spanning multiple taxa, featuring repeats identified in the genomes of 118,070 organisms across all major taxonomic groups. The database currently hosts 30,067,666 inverted repeat sequences, serving as a centralized, user-friendly repository to perform searches, interactive visualization, and download existing inverted repeat data for independent analysis. invertiaDB is implemented as a web portal for browsing, analyzing and downloading inverted repeat data. invertiaDB is publicly available at https://invertiadb.netlify.app/homepage.html.

Lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.), a globally important vegetable crop, is cultivated in various horticultural varieties. Looseleaf lettuce is one of the main varieties that are consumed. Here, we report a telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly of looseleaf lettuce (L. sativa var. crispa cv. Green Elegance). By combining the sequencing data of previously reported Green Elegance v1.2, the 42.20 Gb clean ultra-long reads produced by Oxford Nanopore Technology were used to close the gaps and upgrade the genome assembly. After filling 11 gaps in Green Elegance v1.2, the final gapless telomere-to-telomere genome assembly is 2.58 Gb in length with a contig N50 of 282.47 Mb, containing nine centromeres and 18 telomeres. The genome contained 41,375 protein-coding genes, of which 99.10% were functionally annotated. This T2T genome of looseleaf lettuce will be valuable for the identification of genetic variation and the advancement of lettuce breeding.

Protein domains of transposable elements (TEs) and viruses increase the protein diversity of host genomes by recombining with other protein domains. By screening 10 million eukaryotic proteins, we identified several domains that define multi-copy gene families and frequently co-occur with TE/viral domains. Among these, a Tc1/Mariner transposase helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain was captured by F-box genes in the Caenorhabditis genus, creating a new class of F-box genes. For specific members of this class, like fbxa-215, we found that the HTH domain is required for diverse processes including germ granule localisation, fertility, and thermotolerance. Furthermore, we provide evidence that HSF-1 mediates the transcriptional integration of fbxa-215 into the heat-shock response by binding to Helitron TEs directly upstream of the fbxa-215 locus. The interactome of HTH-bearing F-box factors suggests roles in post-translational regulation and proteostasis, consistent with established functions of F-box proteins. Based on AlphaFold2 multimer proteome-wide screens, we propose that the HTH domain may diversify the repertoire of protein substrates that F-box factors regulate post-translationally. We further demonstrate that F-box genes repeatedly and independently captured TE domains throughout eukaryotic evolution, and describe an additional instance in zebrafish. In conclusion, we identify recurrent TE domain captures by F-box genes in eukaryotes and provide insights into how these novel proteins are integrated within host gene regulatory networks.

Transposable elements (TEs) are abundant selfish genetic elements that can mobilize in their host genome, causing DNA damage, mutations and chromosome rearrangements. TE silencing is thus critical, and is initiated by maternally loaded piRNAs, leading to their repression.

Consistently, paternally inherited TEs are derepressed in the progeny of Drosophila crosses involving a naive female. TEs have also been found to be derepressed in interspecific crosses, which is proposed to result from suboptimal interactions of piRNA pathway proteins. Fundulus heteroclitus and F. diaphanus hybridize in nature and produce viable and fertile offspring that sometimes reproduce asexually. We characterized the repetitive DNA content of these species and their asexually reproducing hybrids. TE load was slightly higher than expected in hybrids and associated with younger repeats. A bi-parentally inherited active Neptune element showed a remarkable [~]4-fold accumulation in hybrids. These results are consistent with suboptimal piRNA pathway function, leading to active TE accumulation.

Rice (Oryza sativa) is one of the most important staple food crops worldwide, and its wild relatives serve as an important gene pool in its breeding. Compared with cultivated rice species, African wild rice (Oryza longistaminata) has several advantageous traits, such as resistance to increased biomass production, clonal propagation via rhizomes, and biotic stresses. However, previous O. longistaminata genome assemblies have been hampered by gaps and incompleteness, restricting detailed investigations into their genomes. To streamline breeding endeavors and facilitate functional genomics studies, we generated a 343-Mb telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly for this species, covering all telomeres and centromeres across the 12 chromosomes. This newly assembled genome has markedly improved over previous versions. Comparative analysis revealed a high degree of synteny with previously published genomes. A large number of structural variations were identified between the O. longistaminata and O. sativa. A total of 2,466 segmentally duplicated genes were identified and enriched in cellular amino acid metabolic processes. We detected a slight expansion of some subfamilies of resistance genes and transcription factors. This newly assembled T2T genome of O. longistaminata provides a valuable resource for the exploration and exploitation of beneficial alleles present in wild relative species of cultivated rice.

sample_q_texts: Despite evidence of evolving fungicide resistance, there is a significant lack of global research and limited solutions for fungal crop pathogens. The rapid spread of anti-fungal fungicide resistance across crop types has made effective, scalable detection and mitigation strategies necessary for sustainable plant protection. Screening of diverse fungal libraries against individual or combinations of fungicides has often been done on single fungal isolates. To enhance fungal and hybrid identification, integrated approaches combining genetic and functional screens are needed. Previously reported 90 genes of a common soybean pathogen Candidatus Liberibacter ssp Spad 20 have been selected by sequencing to produce an expanded comparative screen against fungicide residues. Here we leveraged this screen and pioneered high-throughput phenotyping and functional profiling using 1,664 soybean isolates screened for 98 fungicide-resistant races. Isolation, characterization and functional analysis of 18 superfunctional genes were done. Functional analysis showed a total of 133 genes that were altered and integrated into novel biosynthetic pathways and metabolic shifts. With no mutations in the drug-binding protein genes, all changes occurred through insertions into the genome. Engineered integrated pathways were also developed that enhance responses to fungicide residues. This study not only provides new hypotheses and experimental solutions for crop pathogen identification and functional characterization, but also paves the way for testing and developing new fungicide-based approaches for plant protection.

Knowledge of the identities of the microbes on plant tissues is crucial for developing agroecological programs to enhance crop yield, nutrition, and resistance to pathogens. This is achieved by developing biofortified crops that are genetically modified to accumulate at high levels beneficial microorganisms and secondary metabolites, which may beneficially modify the host. The GMO inhibits the growth of secondary pathogens, hence increases the effectiveness of chemical fertilizers. This global patent-protected technology has gained prominence in the US and several other countries. Its rapid spread is related to the belief that it improves plant resistance to pathogens, accelerates the uptake of fertilizer, increases yields, protects against oxidative stress, and improves vitamin content. However, little has been written about the negative effects of the GMO technology. This review analyses the current implementation of a global patent-protected GMO, challenges, benefits, and disadvantages of its use.

Importing the number sequence tags (INSDs) of plant virus genomes into probabilistic model of immune recognition (Pharmie) revealed that Gynococcus hirticornu (formerly SINB) YP-106 virus strain harbours a nucleoprotein (N-protein) encoded by a pseudogene. The N-protein shares high sequence similarity with the capsid protein (CP) of dicistrich Anthurium solanum and BCP of Tomato Cytisus radicans and IgH of hylaea viridis. Since the 1.2 million amino acid long CP of Dicistrich Anthurium solanum confers resistance to dicistrich C chlorosis the cryptogram present in Gynococcus hirticornu open reading frame was subjected to systematic mutation using random mutagenesis of natural amino acids in vitro using TnRF to compare structural changes and site recognition by the CP. Using heuristic analysis, key residues that dictate CP binding to the cryptogram were placed in an arbitrary position within the CP structure in vitro. The GC content in the RNA pool used for strain mutagenesis was approximately 39 in 1000 nucleotides, suggesting that phage integration occurred with the wild type CP unperturbed by the insertion. Genomes of 5 PCB strains after three in vitro cycles of strain mutagenesis were recovered and the relationship between CP structure and cryptogram was investigated. The test of Gynococcus cryptogram fit and structural property predicted by PSI-BLAST and GNA-seq using amino acid substitution did not match GC homology and structural fit prediction using TnRF. However, re-introduction of the major GC residues in the 5 Gynococcus PCB genomes from the percentage of insertions for each in vitro and their respective CP structure on the basis of structural fit. Mutation-Fit-Align analysis revealed the viruses activated cryptogram did not share common CP sequences within the 5 Gynococcus PCB lineages obtained from the base sequence sequences of 196 APG sequenced genomes from 2009 to 2020, but the Gynococcus CP mutated based on the CP cryptogram fit to the 5 PCB genomes are indicative of cross-site hybridization. Preliminary GC content determined from the set of 5 virus PCB genomes from the region of the CP gene region were ranged from 43.3% to 48.4% with an average of 52.9%. This suggests that the introduction of intronic mutations significantly increases the GC content, with the upper limit being around 60%

Plant and fungal symbioses enable a productive coexistence. In the sugar cane-pathogens interaction, sugar cane stands a favourable symbiont and hosts to vascular wilting syndrome of sugar cane, while pathogens have a prophage to host cancer, which is closely related to fungal symbioses. To gain more insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms and to study the effects of sugar cane wilting syndrome by wood cure-chamber (WCC) treatment on symbioses, we investigated the genes of the fungus Prostephanic acidivorax album and its plants hosts, culicini rosea and oleracea, by ChIP-seq, transcriptome and WB experiments. The main feature of symbioses between woody crops (e.g. rosea) and P. album was highly overlapping from the host-microbe DNA. Both PAR6 and PAR5 and CAI13/ARH7 fused with DNA from rosea. No DNA of CLi1140, CLi1150 and SCCS120 fusion from the fungal endo did not overlap with plant host DNA, but clear overlap was observed between host and fungal DNA. Fusion of CLi1140 and WRKY 7 and also fusion of WT8-C3 and WRKY 3 to plant host DNA were the strongest, followed by WO1, CTS15, WUP1, LHI1, LHI183 and LHI24. In addition, the fusion of RPV1, NWA2, CA/PR15, RPV1, CTS1, WRKY 5, CTS3, WRKY 4, WRKY 14, RPV4, GA2 and BKS1 to plant host DNA was low. Some of them, such as caib1 and RPV1, were not available from gene expression profiles (GEO). The highest coverage of the host-microbe interaction was seen in the case of WUP1, CAI14-2 and CAI13-1 by ChIP-seq. The genome-wide transcriptome analysis revealed that many upregulated transcripts were for carbohydrate metabolism. Analysis of transcript abundances revealed that carbohydrate metabolism is the main focus of these pathways. Also, the protein-coding genes discussed in this study are not linked to sugar cane wilting syndrome, but rather to other symbioses with plant hosts.

Plasmodesmata are tight junctions that allow plant cells to communicate and move solutes. Their function is under-characterised in both plant roots and white clover (Trifolium repens L.). In roots and collards (Brassica oleracea L. var. italica), a two-bladed cornigerini mite (Hybotus Cornigerinus) oviposits in plants and transmits bacteria into xylem. In tricolor clover, ants (Formica sanguinea L.) ingest these bacteria and pass them into root organs. In both cases, bacteria are also expressed and communicate the identity of the donor plant to adjacent cells via O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) transferases (NGTs). However, the subcellular compartment in which NGTs are targeted remains to be established in either Brassica or Trifolium. Here, we establish for the first time that NGT activity is reduced in the root meristem in plants and in shoot meristems in tricolor clover. Analyses demonstrate that this is due to fungal N-acetyltransferase (FANT) deficiency that leads to a blocked processing of pre-NAGs from intracellular glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH). NGTs and NGT-associated DNAase activity (NDA) are not affected. This reduction of fungal NGTs is due to an absence of fungal N-acetyltransferase genes. Analysis of NGTs-encoded DNA degradation products demonstrate that FANT-mediated degradation does not directly trigger de novo DNA strand breaks in the gene targets, though it clearly allows disruption of DNA integrity in root xylem and trigger filamin A polymerisation (FAP). We conclude that interference in NGT biosynthesis and/or degradation leads to deficiency of NAD-dependent plant protein phosphatase (PpAP) activity and, ultimately, of plant NGT-encoded Dicer activity. This reduces NGT activity, which could thus impair NGT functionality in primary cells. Consistently, plants lacking FANT are unable to defend themselves from invading nematodes. Our findings underscore the fact that bacteria can infect, or indirectly drive, the growth of endosymbiotic plant bacteria, and that transmission is directed through plants xylem tissue. We demonstrate that fungal NGTs are essential for infection defence.

Plant pathogens often release toxins to suppress, capture, or eradicate their hosts. Whether Pseudomonas putida mass shoots seed mass to bacteroides-free plants is unknown. Using an antibiotic-, anthelmintic- and melittodoner-free testing system, we found that at least 1162 Pseudomonas putida strains harbor the antitoxin sequence Q. A test for Q. suppressor induced in bacterial can also be used to test for R. suppressors. The identification of Q. suppressor-related genes, including those associated with PPP-ABC and papain pathways, enabled us to isolate, identify, and characterize the PPP-enzyme reductase PPH-C from P. putida inhibitors of the endogenous phytoalexin 11-oxo-phytolcin F. Enzyme activities and fluorescence were used to characterize pph-C as a protease family member that is predominantly localized to vesicles. To establish the primary role of pph-C as a protease in suppressing and eradicating plant growth, cell free extracts from the mutants identified by the inhibitor selection assay were used to inactivate P. putida. Bioinformatically, pph-C is likely to have been evolved specifically as a protease. In the last part of this study, we reveal the prototype for each of the distinct PP pillin subtypes proposed for P. putida.

SignificancePlant pathogens develop and use defensive strategies to suppress, eradicate, or eliminate their hosts. Using bioinformatically identified PP pillin and PPP gene and gene family members, we could specifically isolate and characterize the culprit hydrolytic enzyme, thereby furthering our understanding of different peptide pillins and elucidating the functions of their hypothetical pharmaceutical mimicry. These studies serve as a proof of concept to accurately predict the potential utility of peptide pillins in plant resistance and target discovery as well as to identify the key proteins and enzymes involved in the suppression and eradication of plant hosts.

Plants maintain homeostasis by adjusting their susceptibility to pathogens and interacting with the environment. To exert this, they often leverage their plants innate immune systems, a component of the plant immune system that develops via natural selection. For example, Arabidopsis thaliana cell-cell communication mediated by a neuron-like immune suppressor Lsr1 is present in wild-type plants, and is diminished in mutants of Lsr1 by the TCR cascade. The hyper-tight interaction and diversity of the Lsr1 immune suppressor E-cadherin, together with its production by NtrA and Cue1, negatively affect integrated defense responses such as the leaf-based signaling pathway involved in leaf pathogen response. These signals are dominated by salicylic acid and regulated by the Arabidopsis REB protein, which couples salicylic acid with calcium signal transduction and the flower type-specific protein ATF6.

Here, we show a striking deficiency in the attenuated Arabidopsis Clonal Protoplast Culture (APCP) T1 immune suppressors, Lsr1, the E-cadherin pathway (Theps), and ATF6, that are induced following infection by citrus chlorosis disease (CCD) causing the RNA virus Citrus Brittle Rot Virus (BRV). The defense response of Lsr1, E-cadherin, and ATF6 is highly conserved, and down-regulation of Clavell (CAV) and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4PDB), both cis-acting to CACNB1, leads to their lethal infection of the APCP T1 cell line. A number of molecular mechanisms linking Lsr1 to the defense response are discussed.

Plants defend against pathogenic microbial attack via cellular signaling cascades leading to cell lysis and systemic infection. Accurate recognition of species based on genetic markers, however, is hindered by limited level of species and molecular diversity and lack of phenotypic plasticity in many plant species. This hinders efficient pathogen detection, epidemiological modelling, and biological control, hindering the adoption of new resistance genes into crop species to mitigate disease severity. Here we describe our work to develop an algorithm that successfully classifies pathogens based on their amino acid sequence. The algorithm uses supervised machine learning to train a feed-forward artificial neural network with a handcrafted feature descriptor based on repetitive unit rules generated by restriction-modification analysis of plants. The algorithm achieved 94% classification accuracy in classifying a selection of samples of pathogens and the characters coded as representative of the original bacterial species. Furthermore, the algorithm was demonstrated to be successful with a traditional knowledge-base to classify and find a specific pathogen. These results demonstrate an approach that can be used to detect pathogens using machine learning methods, with the potential to speed up research and regulatory timelines in the sector.

Plant pathogens and disease suppressants are selectively accumulated throughout the life history of plants to allow speedy growth and development following infection. To achieve rapid adaptation and pathogen suppression, plants should balance resources and fitness, which can be achieved by exploiting resources from their environment and suppressing potential pathogens by inducing a delay to growth and development. The effects of 12-phospho-deoxytolytase (PPT) (PPTase), an enzyme that produces proline in plants, on plant growth and susceptibility to rice common bunt, Colletotrichum musae, were investigated by removing the PPTase enzyme from rice seedlings. The PPTase knockout line (PPT-KO) developed an altered growth pattern. The seedlings did not grow beyond the 1st leaf stage. Morphological symptoms showed lower interveinal tissues, pale root and cuticle, and elevated needle number. PPT-KO seedlings also demonstrated a diminished resistance to common bunt. Our results demonstrate the changes in growth patterns resulting from a loss of PPTase in rice.

The Spatzinum inducers Lymantria dispar were observed to exclusively cleave NF-B, while Cyrtodactylus inaequiline and strains belonging to their species have also been shown to cleave NF-B with different efficiencies. However, the gene-based variations of these NF-B cleavages in Lymantria dispar against different inducer targets has not been comprehensively studied. Here, we presented single-cell transcriptomic profiles and single-molecule sequencing for NF-B knockdown and NF-B protection experiments in two cultured L. dispar populations, - endogenously silenced by orthologous wild-type (WT) and lower expressed (Lv) alleles - and the in vitro (S69) and ex vivo (342/1) cell lines generated by Zhang [Yu, F. et al. (2018). Bull. Entomol. Res. 68(1):40-51.](1) e164. The genetic/phenotypic difference between LV and WT populations shows LD fractionation signatures, indicative of reduced polymorphism. NF-B knockdown in these two cultures, either by Lymantria dispar indoles or sodium azide, promotes greater binding to cyt c at the NF-B binding pocket as compared to NF-B expression level, whereas NF-B protection induced by sodium azide promotes more binding to Nbs1 complex. In-cell transcriptomic gene-expression profiling and probing of NF-B proteins show the lowest clustering of gene profiles in cells where NF-B mRNA is modified compared to (Lv) WT. Interestingly, NF-B cleavage by Lymantria dispar may promote mRNA stability through modulation of protein acetylation at Nbs1 complex. In summary, our studies demonstrate that NF-B signals control not only pathways downstream of NF-B, but also the environment in which the NF-B pathway is turned on.
sample_p_texts: Rust fungi comprise thousands of species many of which cause disease on important crop plants. The flax rust fungus Melampsora lini has been a model species for the genetic dissection of plant immunity since the 1940s, however the highly fragmented and incomplete reference genome has so far hindered progress in effector gene discovery. Here, we generate a fully-phased, chromosome-scale assembly of the two nuclear genomes of M. lini strain CH5, resolving an additional 320 Mbp of sequence compared to the previous short-read assembly. The 482 Mbp dikaryotic genome is at least 79% repetitive with a large proportion ([~]40%) of the genome comprised of young, highly similar transposable elements. The assembly resolves the known effector gene loci some of which carry complex duplications that were collapsed in the previous assembly. Using a genetic map followed by manual correction of gene models, we identify the AvrM3 and AvrN genes which encode unusually large fungal effector proteins and trigger defense responses when co-expressed with the corresponding resistance genes in Nicotiana tabacum. We locate the genes linked to the tetrapolar mating system on chromosomes 4 and 9, but in contrast to the cereal rusts which have one pheromone receptor gene per haplotype, in flax rust three pheromone receptor genes are found with two of them closely linked on one haplotype. Taken together, we show that a high-quality assembly is crucial for resolving complex gene loci and given the increasing number of fungal effectors of large size, the commonly applied criterion for effector candidates as being small proteins as needs to be reconsidered.

O_LIPhytoplasmas are specialized phloem-limited bacteria that cause diseases on various crops resulting in significant agricultural losses. This research focuses on the jujube Witches Broom (JWB) phytoplasma and investigates the host-manipulating activity of the effector SJP39.
C_LIO_LIWe found that SJP39 directly interacts with the plant transcription factor bHLH87 in the nuclei. SJP39 stabilizes the bHLH87 homologs in A. thaliana and jujube, leading to growth defects in the plants.
C_LIO_LITranscriptomic analysis indicates that SJP39 affects the gibberellin (GA) pathway in jujube. We further demonstrate that ZjbHLH87 regulates GA signalling as a negative regulator and SJP39 enhances this regulation.
C_LIO_LIThe research offers important insights into the pathogenesis of JWB disease and identified SJP39 as a virulence factor that can contribute to the growth defects caused by JWB phytoplasma infection. These findings open new opportunities to manage JWB and other phytoplasma diseases.
